units: Interstate 5 begins at the Mexican border, at the San Ysidro Port of Entry, which federal officials call the busiest land port in the Western Hemisphere.
On a typical day about 70,000 vehicles and 20,000 people on foot enter the United States here from Tijuana, with cars lining up across 34 lanes.
This is the homeland of the Kumeyaay Nation.
Kumeyaay country runs from the Pacific to the Colorado River, and along the coast from about Oceanside to south of Ensenada, so since 1848 the international border has run right through it.
Kumeyaay people live on both sides today, with 13 bands in San Diego County and more communities in Baja California.

The Tijuana River rises in the mountains of Baja California, runs through Tijuana in a concrete channel, and crosses into the United States near here for its last few miles to the sea.
Its mouth, the Tijuana River Estuary, is Southern California's largest coastal wetland, where more than 370 kinds of birds have been seen.
The river also carries Tijuana's sewage overflows, and in 2013 beaches near its mouth were closed for 204 days.

East of the freeway, a 93-foot stainless steel test wing for a World War II bomber stands on end.
Locals sometimes call it the Silver Wing.
It honors John J. Montgomery, who in the spring of 1884 made glider flights of up to 600 feet from the rim of Otay Mesa.
He never claimed to be first, but some historians count these as the first controlled flights of a heavier-than-air craft in America.

In 1915, San Diego's city council voted to pay Charles Hatfield, a self-styled rainmaker, $10,000 to fill a reservoir.
In January 1916 the rain came and kept coming.
On January 27 the Lower Otay Dam burst and sent a wall of water 40 feet high down the Otay River valley, which meets San Diego Bay near here.
The flood reportedly killed about 20 people, though accounts vary, among them 11 Japanese American farmers.
On the bay side of the freeway, ocean water sits in ponds until the sun dries it into salt.
People have harvested salt here since at least 1871, which makes the South Bay Salt Works the second-longest-running business in San Diego, after the San Diego Union-Tribune newspaper.
Its ponds cover more than a thousand acres and yield about 75,000 tons of salt a year.
Chula Vista, the old Lemon Capital.
Chula Vista is Spanish for beautiful view, a name suggested by the designer of the Sweetwater Dam.
Water from that dam, finished in 1888, irrigated the farmland here, and for a time Chula Vista was the largest lemon-growing center in the world.
By 1911 about 4,000 acres were lemon groves, and the town was once known as the Lemon Capital of the World.
West of the freeway, where the Sweetwater River meets San Diego Bay, 316 acres of salt marsh and coastal upland form part of a national wildlife refuge.
More than 90 percent of the bay's old wetlands have been filled, drained or diked, which is why this piece matters.
The refuge breeds endangered light-footed Ridgway's rails, and it is the only place in the United States where a plant called yerba reuma grows wild.
National City takes its name from a ranch.
Spanish soldiers grazed their horses on 26,000 acres here called El Rancho del Rey, the Ranch of the King.
After Mexico won independence it became Rancho de la Nación, the Ranch of the Nation.
In 1868 three Kimball brothers from San Francisco bought the whole rancho and kept the name National for the town they founded.
The Navy ships along the bay belong to Naval Base San Diego, the main home port of the US Pacific Fleet.
More than 50 ships tie up at its 13 piers, and over 24,000 military personnel and 10,000 civilians work on the base.
It is the second-largest surface ship base in the world, after Naval Station Norfolk.
The long, curving bridge over the bay is the San Diego-Coronado Bridge, opened in 1969.
The Navy wanted 200 feet of clearance for its ships, so the bridge curves 80 degrees to gain enough length to climb that high at a reasonable grade.
Under its ramps, beside this freeway, lies Chicano Park, home to the largest collection of outdoor murals in the United States.
El Indio began in 1940 as a family tortilla shop, and since 1947 it has served food from a spot on India Street that now sits beside the freeway.
During World War II, workers from the aircraft factory across the street asked founder Ralph Pesqueira Sr. for a portable lunch.
He adapted his Sonoran grandmother's recipe for flautas, and he claimed credit for naming the little rolled tacos taquitos.
Jets landing at San Diego International Airport make a steep descent over the crest of Bankers Hill, close to the downtown towers, to reach a single runway.
It is the busiest single-runway airport in the United States.
Because the airport is so close, federal rules since the 1970s have kept downtown buildings to 500 feet or less, which is why the skyline looks so even.
The hill east of the freeway is Presidio Hill, where Spain founded its first fort and mission in California in 1769, above Kosa'aay, a Kumeyaay village of 30 to 40 families.
In the 1820s, settlers moved down to the foot of the hill and started a town.
That town is preserved as Old Town San Diego State Historic Park, with five original adobes, and the park and its museums are free to enter.

Exit 20 is Interstate 8 east, the way to Mission San Diego de Alcalá, about eight miles inland.
Founded in 1769, it was the first of California's 21 missions and is still a working parish.
This valley is Kumeyaay homeland, and in 1775 people from several Kumeyaay villages burned the mission.

Mission Bay and San Diego River.
The San Diego River, crossed by the freeway near here, ends at the sea beside Mission Bay.
The explorer Cabrillo named this water False Bay in 1542, when it was a shifting maze of lagoons and tidal marsh.
Starting in the late 1940s, dredges moved 25 million cubic yards of sand and silt to build the islands and coves of Mission Bay Park, the largest man-made aquatic park in the country.
The big hill west of the freeway is Mount Soledad, 823 feet high, with a 29-foot cross and TV towers on top.
Its steep north and east slopes rise along the Rose Canyon Fault, which runs north from downtown San Diego beneath this freeway.
The fault's last big quake probably struck in the 1700s, before the missions were built, and scientists estimate it produces a magnitude 6.9 quake about every 700 years on average.
The white building with two tall spires beside the freeway is the San Diego California Temple of the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints.
Dedicated in 1993, it was the church's third temple in California.
Its spires rise about 200 feet, and a gold-leaf statue of the angel Moroni stands on top of the eastern one.
West of the freeway, Los Peñasquitos Lagoon, Spanish for the little cliffs, spreads about 500 acres of marsh beside bluffs where Torrey pines grow, the rarest pine in North America.
This kind grows wild only here and on a small strip just north in Del Mar.
Sea winds twist the exposed trees into shapes like giant bonsai.
The racetrack and fairgrounds beside the San Dieguito River are where the turf meets the surf.
Singer Bing Crosby and businessman William Quigley founded the track, and on opening day, July 3, 1937, Crosby himself stood at the main gate welcoming 15,000 fans.
The 370-acre grounds are also home to the San Diego County Fair.
The freeway crosses San Elijo Lagoon, a 915-acre reserve where Escondido Creek meets the sea.
The Portolá expedition named it San Alejo, for Saint Alexius, in 1769.
When this freeway was built in 1965, its earth berm squeezed the tides.
The freeway and rail bridges have since been rebuilt with wider spans, and restored channels now let up to three times more water flow in and out with each tide.
Encinitas is Spanish for little oaks.
In 1769 the Portolá expedition met people from the Kumeyaay village of Jeyal near San Elijo Lagoon and named this valley Los Encinos, for its oak forest.
A Mexican land grant called Rancho Las Encinitas followed in 1842, and today's city formed in 1986 from five communities, including Cardiff-by-the-Sea, Leucadia and Olivenhain.
The Ecke family moved their poinsettia business from Los Angeles to Encinitas in 1923, buying 40 acres at $150 an acre.
By grafting two varieties together they grew fuller, bushier plants, and until the 1990s they had a virtual monopoly on the Christmas flower.
As late as 2008, the family business still served about half the world market and 70 percent of the American one.
The freeway crosses Batiquitos Lagoon, 610 acres of tidal wetland where San Marcos Creek meets the sea.
Its name comes from batequi, a northwestern Mexican word for a watering hole dug in a streambed, borrowed from the Yaqui language.
People have lived around this lagoon for more than 9,000 years.
In spring, the hillside east of the freeway turns bright with flowers.
These are The Flower Fields, 55 acres of Giant Tecolote ranunculus, which bloom for six to eight weeks from early March into early May.
The farm sits on a slope overlooking the Pacific and is open to visitors from March 1 until about Mother's Day.
The strawberry fields beside the freeway at Cannon Road belong to the Carlsbad Strawberry Company, a pick-your-own farm run by third-generation farmer Jimmy Ukegawa.
Seedlings go in each October, the first berries come around the start of the year, and picking season usually runs from March through July.
Agua Hedionda and the desal plant.
The freeway crosses Agua Hedionda Lagoon, Spanish for fetid water.
Beside it, near the beach, the Claude Bud Lewis Carlsbad Desalination Plant opened in 2015 as the largest in the Western Hemisphere.
It draws in about 100 million gallons of seawater a day and pushes it through reverse osmosis filters, turning half into drinking water, about 7 percent of what the San Diego region uses.
Carlsbad is named for a spa town in Bohemia.
In the 1880s a former sailor, John Frazier, dug a well here and offered its water at the train stop, which became known as Frazier's Station.

Tests on a second well found the water chemically similar to that of some of the world's most famous spas, so the town was named for the Bohemian spa of Karlsbad, now Karlovy Vary in the Czech Republic.
The freeway crosses Buena Vista Lagoon, the 223-acre border between Carlsbad and Oceanside and California's first ecological reserve.
A weir about 100 yards from the beach holds it back from the sea, so unlike its neighbors it is a freshwater lagoon.
At least 103 kinds of birds have been seen here, and fall brings migrating flocks.
Oceanside's wooden pier, 1,942 feet long, is the second-longest wooden pier on the West Coast.
The first one went up in 1888, the year the city incorporated, and storms have wrecked it again and again.
Today's pier, the sixth, opened in 1987.
In April 2024 a fire destroyed the old diner at its far end, and rebuilding was expected to begin in 2027.

Exit 54 is Highway 76 east, the way to Mission San Luis Rey, about four and a half miles inland.
Founded in 1798, it grew to be the largest of California's missions and is nicknamed the King of the Missions.
It lies in the homeland of the Payómkawichum, the people the Spanish named Luiseño.

The open hills along this stretch belong to Marine Corps Base Camp Pendleton, more than 125,000 acres with 17 miles of coastline, the last major undeveloped stretch of California coast south of Santa Barbara.
It was Rancho Santa Margarita y Las Flores until 1942, when the Marines turned it into a training base for World War II.
The freeway crosses the Santa Margarita River, one of the last free-flowing rivers in Southern California.
It runs about 31 miles from near Temecula to the sea, and its lower 10 miles spread into a wide floodplain across Camp Pendleton.
The Portolá expedition camped beside it on July 20, 1769, and named it for Saint Margaret of Antioch.
The railroad beside the freeway through Camp Pendleton is the Surf Line, named because in places it runs within 100 feet of the Pacific.
Finished from Oceanside to Santa Ana in 1888, it became the only line into San Diego from the north after floods wrecked the first route inland.
Today it is the second-busiest passenger rail corridor in the United States.
Near the Las Pulgas Road exit stands the Las Flores Adobe, a big U-shaped ranch house built in 1867 and 1868 by Marco Forster and now a National Historic Landmark.
It sits where Mission San Luis Rey set up a way station in 1823, halfway to Mission San Juan Capistrano.
Las Pulgas means the fleas, after a mission survey party that camped in the canyon and got badly bitten.
On the lanes toward San Clemente, about seven miles south of that city, stands a permanent Border Patrol checkpoint, one of 33 fixed checkpoints near the Mexican border.
Agents may briefly stop and question drivers here without any particular suspicion.
The Supreme Court upheld that power in 1976 in United States v.
Martinez-Fuerte, a case that began with a stop at this checkpoint.
The San Onofre nuclear power plant, on the beach here, was long known for its two giant round domes, the containment buildings around its reactors.
Its last two reactors were shut down in January 2012, after early wear turned up on more than 3,000 tubes in new steam generators, and in 2013 Southern California Edison retired the plant for good.
Crews are taking it apart, and removal of the domes was set to begin in 2027, so they may be partly or entirely gone.
San Onofre, Spanish for Saint Onuphrius, a hermit from fourth-century Egypt, is a 3,000-acre state beach on Marine Corps land leased to California, with more than 2.5 million visitors a year.
Surfers on redwood boards came here by the 1940s.
Its northern surf breaks, called Trestles, are named for a wooden railroad trestle that surfers walked under to reach the beach.
Lower Trestles hosted the pro surfing world tour for many years, and Trestles is set to host the 2028 Olympic surfing contests.
On the bluff at Cotton's Point stands La Casa Pacifica, the house of peace, which President Richard Nixon bought in 1969.
The press nicknamed it the Western White House.
Soviet leader Leonid Brezhnev and the president of Mexico visited, and after Nixon resigned he retired here to write his memoirs.
The road beside the freeway nearby is named Avenida del Presidente, the Avenue of the President.
Inland of the freeway, in the San Mateo campground area of San Onofre State Beach, is Panhe, the place at the water.
It was one of the largest Acjachemen villages, more than 8,000 years old, with perhaps 300 people when the Spanish arrived.
It remains a sacred, ceremonial and burial site for the Acjachemen people, who hold a festival there each year to honor their ancestors.
In 1925 Ole Hanson, a former mayor of Seattle, laid out a 2,000-acre town on old rancho land by the ocean and named it after San Clemente Island.
He added a clause to the deeds sending every building plan to an architectural review board, to keep roofs of red tile and walls of white.
The rule did not last, but the city still calls itself the Spanish Village by the Sea.
West of the freeway on Pacific Coast Highway, Dana Point is named for Richard Henry Dana Jr., who sailed here in 1835 on the brig Pilgrim and wrote about it in Two Years Before the Mast.
Cowhides from Mission San Juan Capistrano were brought to the cliffs, and sailors flung them out to the beach below, a job Dana compared to flying a kite without a string.

Exit 82 is Ortega Highway, and Mission San Juan Capistrano is less than a mile west of it.
Founded in 1776, it is famous for its swallows and for the ruins of the Great Stone Church, which fell in an earthquake in 1812.

Just off the freeway, about a mile north of the mission, stood Putuidem, a mother village of the Acjachemen people that gave rise to other villages.
Its name means belly or navel.

In a story of the village, the chief's daughter Coronne died suddenly and her body became a mound of earth, and the grieving people slept in a pyramid shape called acjachema, which gave the Acjachemen their name.
The freeway crosses Arroyo Trabuco here, a 22-mile creek that runs out of the Santa Ana Mountains to meet San Juan Creek beside the mission.
Trabuco is Spanish for blunderbuss, a kind of old shotgun.
The story goes that in July 1769 a soldier with the Portolá expedition, camped on a bluff above the creek, found his blunderbuss missing.
It was never found, and the creek was named for it.
East of San Juan Capistrano, between Ladera Ranch and San Clemente, lies Rancho Mission Viejo, the old mission ranch, still about 23,000 acres.
Irish immigrants Richard O'Neill and James Flood bought it after its owner died in 1882, and under O'Neill it became Orange County's largest wheat producer.
His descendants still run it as a working ranch, with cattle, orchards and a nature reserve.
On clear days, the two-humped mountain east of the freeway is Saddleback.
Its higher summit, Santiago Peak, rises 5,689 feet, the highest point in Orange County, and its crown of antennas sends radio signals across much of five counties.
The lower summit, Modjeska Peak, less than a mile away, is named for Helena Modjeska, a Polish stage star who lived in a canyon at its foot in her later years.
El Toro Y. This is the El Toro Y, where Interstate 5 and Interstate 405 meet.
It is named for the old town of El Toro, Spanish for the bull, which renamed itself Lake Forest in 1991, and for the Marine air station next door.
From 1975 to 2002, traffic here more than tripled, to 356,000 vehicles a day, and after a widening finished in 1997 the road here was 26 lanes wide.
East of the freeway, the Marines flew from El Toro air station from 1942 until it closed in 1999.
The Marine Corps paid James Irvine $100,000 for 4,000 acres of his ranch, land that then held the largest lima bean field in North America.
Its runways could take the biggest planes in the military, and while the base was open, every president since World War II landed here in Air Force One.
The land around here was part of the Irvine Ranch, which once stretched 23 miles from the ocean to the Santa Ana River.
James Irvine and his partners began it in 1864 from old Mexican land grants, after a drought killed a rancher's livestock and forced him to sell.
By 1918 the ranch grew 60,000 acres of lima beans, and in the 1960s its fields began turning into the planned city of Irvine.
Jamboree Road is named for a Boy Scout campout.
In 1953 the Irvine Company let the National Scout Jamboree use ranch land where Newport Beach's Fashion Island now stands, the first national jamboree held west of the Mississippi.
Thousands of tents went up on land reached only by a muddy two-lane trail, which was soon paved and later renamed Jamboree Road.
South of the freeway stands one of two giant wooden hangars the Navy built during World War II for blimps that patrolled the coast.
The surviving south hangar is more than 1,000 feet long and 17 stories tall, one of the largest wooden structures ever built.
Its twin, the north hangar, burned in a fire on November 7, 2023.
In 1936 Orange County grew a sixth of the nation's Valencia oranges, and by 1948 it had 67,263 acres of them, more than five million trees.
In 1949 alone, nearly 7,000 acres of orange trees disappeared, and each year more fell as housing tracts spread.
By 1985 fewer than 4,000 acres of Valencias were left, mostly on the Irvine Ranch, and twenty years later fewer than 100.
Right beside the freeway, in Prentice Park, is the Santa Ana Zoo, which opened on March 8, 1952.
Joseph Prentice gave the city the land in 1949 on the condition that the zoo keep at least 50 monkeys at all times.
It keeps more than a dozen kinds of primates, and it focuses on the animals and plants of Central and South America.
West of the freeway, Santa Ana grew on Rancho Santiago de Santa Ana, granted in 1810 to José Antonio Yorba, a sergeant in the Spanish army.
His rancho took in the land of today's Santa Ana, Orange, Tustin, Irvine and Costa Mesa.
The modern town was founded in 1869 and became the seat of the new Orange County in 1889.
In 1877 it offered the Southern Pacific $10,000 and free land to end its new rail line here instead of in Tustin, and won.
The wide channel under the freeway here is the Santa Ana River, the largest river entirely within Southern California, running 96 miles from the San Bernardino Mountains to the sea.
Soldiers with the Portolá expedition named it Río de Santa Ana in July 1769, probably because they had just celebrated Saint Anne's Day.
The city and the mountains took their names from the river.
The huge glass building west of the freeway is Christ Cathedral, built as the Crystal Cathedral and finished in 1980.
Its 10,000 rectangular panes are mirrored outside and see-through inside, and when it opened it was described as the largest glass building in the world.
Despite the name, no crystal glass was used.
Since 2019 it has been the cathedral of the Catholic Diocese of Orange.
Angel Stadium and the Big A. East of the freeway, near Katella Avenue, is Angel Stadium, home of the Los Angeles Angels since 1966.
Among major league ballparks still in use, only Fenway Park, Wrigley Field and Dodger Stadium are older.
From 1980 to 1994 the Los Angeles Rams played football here too.
At the edge of the parking lot, beside Highway 57, stands the Big A, a 230-foot sign with a halo near the top.
Just southwest of the freeway is Disneyland, built on 160 acres of orange groves and walnut trees, a site picked by researchers Disney hired to forecast where the region's population would grow.
Construction began in July 1954, while this freeway, then U.S. 101, was being built just north of the site, and two extra lanes were added for the expected crowds.
The park opened one year and one day later, on July 17, 1955.
Anaheim was founded in 1857 by 50 German families from San Francisco, who bought some 1,160 acres near the Santa Ana River for 2 dollars an acre to grow grapes.
They named it Annaheim, home by the Santa Ana River.
Most of them were carpenters and craftsmen who had never made wine, yet for about 25 years the area was the largest wine producer in California.
About a mile and a half south on Beach Boulevard, Knott's Berry Farm began in 1923 as a roadside berry stand.
In the late 1920s Walter Knott helped a federal berry expert hunt for a big berry grown by Rudolph Boysen, and on Boysen's old farm they found a few frail vines in a field choked with weeds.
Knott nursed them back to health, sold the big berries at his stand from 1932, and called them boysenberries after their originator.
La Mirada, Spanish for the look, began as the ranch of Andrew McNally, the Chicago printer and mapmaker of Rand McNally.
In 1888 he bought more than 2,200 acres for $200,000 and surrounded his home, Windermere Ranch, with olive, orange and lemon groves.
He built a plant to press fine olive oil and a railroad station to ship his oil and fruit across the country.
In 1784 the Spanish governor gave a former soldier, Manuel Nieto, the use of all the land between the Santa Ana and Los Angeles rivers, from Mission San Gabriel down to the sea.
Rancho Los Nietos started at about 300,000 acres, one of the first and largest Spanish land concessions in California.
Norwalk, Downey, Buena Park, Anaheim, Whittier and Long Beach all sit on parts of it today.
Santa Fe Springs takes its name from mineral springs that Dr. James Fulton turned into a sulfur spa in the 1870s, and that the Santa Fe Railway bought in 1886.
In 1921 a well called Union-Bell blew in as a 2,500-barrel gusher and set off an oil rush.
Within a year the field was considered one of the richest in petroleum history, and in the 1920s it produced as much as 345,000 barrels a day.
San Gabriel River and Rio Hondo.
The freeway crosses the San Gabriel River here, beside the 605 junction, and the Rio Hondo, Spanish for deep river, about two and a half miles to the northwest.
The two run about two miles apart and were once one restless system.
Before levees, the San Gabriel jumped between outlets with winter storms, and after a flood in the late 1860s it cut a new course, leaving its old bed to become the Rio Hondo.
Downey, southwest of the freeway, is named for John Gately Downey, the youngest governor California ever had.
Its big aircraft plant, run by North American Aviation, built all of the Apollo command and service modules, nine of which carried astronauts to the Moon.
Less than a mile down Lakewood Boulevard stands the oldest McDonald's, a walk-up stand from 1953 that still has its original golden arches, two tall arches of sheet metal.
That long wall decorated like an ancient palace was built in 1929 as the Samson Tire and Rubber Company factory.
Its architects modeled it on the castle of the Assyrian king Sargon II, in a style called Exotic Revival, and the same firm designed the Mayan Theater in Los Angeles.
Tires were made here until 1978, and the old factory front is now the face of the Citadel Outlets.
The towers of downtown Los Angeles rise to the west, across the Los Angeles River.
The one with a thin spire on top is the Wilshire Grand Center, finished in 2017.
Counting the spire it stands 1,100 feet, the tallest building in the United States west of Chicago, though the U.S. Bank Tower's roof is higher.
Many towers around it have flat tops because a 1974 city fire rule required rooftop helipads on tall buildings.
The tall Art Deco tower near the interchange belongs to the old Sears, Roebuck mail-order building, finished in 1927 in just 171 days.
Its nine stories held about 11 acres of floor space, shipping catalog orders to the Rocky Mountain and Pacific Coast states.
Over the years its 226-foot tower and Sears sign were called a beacon for Eastsiders returning home on the freeways.
This tangle of ramps is the East Los Angeles Interchange, where Interstate 5, Interstate 10, U.S. 101 and State Route 60 meet on 135 acres of Boyle Heights.
A 2008 count put more than 550,000 vehicles a day through its southern part, and it is often called the busiest freeway interchange in the world.
Radio traffic reporter Bill Keene called it Malfunction Junction.
At exit 135, Interstate 10 heads about 8 miles east to Mission San Gabriel.
Exit 135 is the ramp to Interstate 10 east, the way to Mission San Gabriel, about eight miles away in the city of San Gabriel.
Founded in 1771, it stands in Tongva homeland, and about 6,000 Native people are buried on its grounds.
In 1785 a medicine woman named Toypurina helped organize a revolt against the mission.

Across the river, where downtown Los Angeles now stands, was Yaanga, recorded as the largest and most influential Tongva village in the region.
At its center grew a great sycamore later called El Aliso, a landmark known to traders from as far away as present-day Yuma.
The Portolá expedition reached Yaanga in 1769, and in 1781 Spanish settlers founded the pueblo of Los Angeles next to it.
The freeway crosses the Los Angeles River here, where the Arroyo Seco flows in, and meets the Arroyo Seco Parkway, one of the oldest freeways in the United States.
It was dedicated on December 30, 1940, and opened the next day, in time for crowds heading to the Rose Parade and Rose Bowl in Pasadena.
It was the first road built under a 1939 California law that let the state limit access to a few set points.
The wooded hills beside the freeway are Elysian Park, created in 1886 and, at 600 acres, one of the largest parks in Los Angeles.
Tucked into them is Chavez Ravine, home of Dodger Stadium.

By the 1940s the ravine held three close-knit, mostly Mexican American neighborhoods, La Loma, Palo Verde and Bishop, where many families lived because of housing discrimination elsewhere in the city.
The channel beside the freeway is the Los Angeles River.
Most of it was lined with concrete after the deadly flood of 1938, but in this 11-mile stretch, the Glendale Narrows, the groundwater sits so high that the bottom was left unpaved.
That is why willows, reeds and sandbars grow right in the river.
The brushy hills west of the freeway are Griffith Park, more than 4,000 acres of chaparral and parkland that the city calls the largest urban-wilderness municipal park in the United States.
On December 16, 1896, Griffith J. Griffith gave the first 3,015 acres to the people of Los Angeles as a Christmas gift.
On October 3, 1933, a brush fire in Griffith Park killed at least 29 men who volunteered or were ordered to fight it.
Thousands of workers on a federally funded project were in the park that day, clearing brush and building trails for 40 cents an hour.
The fire burned only about 47 acres, yet for 85 years it was the deadliest wildfire in California history.
Three family stops sit along the north side of Griffith Park:
the Los Angeles Zoo, the Autry Museum of the American West, and Travel Town, a railroad museum with 43 full-size engines, cars and other rolling stock.
Actor Gene Autry founded his museum of the West here in 1988.
Just east of the freeway stands the 1928 terminal building of Grand Central Airport, once a major gateway to Los Angeles by air.
In July 1929 it became the western end of the Lindbergh Line, a 48-hour coast-to-coast trip with planes by day and trains by night.
The old runway is now a city street, Grand Central Avenue.
The rocky range rising east of the freeway is the Verdugo Mountains, topping out at 3,126 feet.
They are named for José María Verdugo, a Spanish soldier who came north with the 1769 expedition and in 1784 received Rancho San Rafael, about 36,000 acres that now hold Glendale and Burbank.
Burbank, which the freeway passes through, is commonly known as the Media Capital of the World.
Warner Bros. and the Walt Disney Company both have their headquarters here, in the Media District, a couple of miles west of the freeway.
Warner Bros. took over the First National studio lot in 1928, and Disney, after the success of Snow White and the Seven Dwarfs, finished its Burbank studio on Buena Vista Street in 1939.
During World War II, Lockheed's aircraft factory beside the Burbank airport was disguised from the air.
It was covered with a huge painted tarp showing a quiet country neighborhood, with rubber cars and hundreds of fake trees made of chicken wire and feathers.
Lockheed and its Vega company built 19,278 planes during the war.
Long before it was Sun Valley, this was Wixánga, a Fernandeño Tongva village whose name means something like place of the thorns, for the prickly pear cactus growing here.
The Spanish name, Cañada de las Tunas, carried the same idea and survives in nearby La Tuna Canyon.
Later the area was called Roscoe, and in 1950 residents chose the name Sun Valley.
In 1874, J. B. Lankershim and Isaac Van Nuys began dry-farming wheat across the southern half of the San Fernando Valley.
By 1876 the valley was the biggest wheat-growing area in Los Angeles County, and that year they sent the first wheat shipment from San Pedro Harbor to Europe.
Pacoima takes its name from Pakoinga, the name of a Native village here meaning entrance; Spanish ears heard its ng sound as an m.
It is also the hometown of Ritchie Valens, born Richard Valenzuela here in 1941, who turned the Mexican folk song La Bamba into a rock and roll hit in 1958.
At exit 157, San Fernando Mission Boulevard heads about 1.1 miles west to Mission San Fernando.
Exit 157 is San Fernando Mission Boulevard, and Mission San Fernando is about a mile west of it.
Founded in 1797, the mission gave its name to the San Fernando Valley.
The people who lived and worked here included Tataviam, Tongva and Chumash families.

The reservoirs just west of the freeway once supplied about 80 percent of Los Angeles' water.
When the San Fernando earthquake struck on February 9, 1971, part of the Lower Van Norman Dam slid into its reservoir, leaving only about 5 feet of dam above the water.
Eighty thousand people living below it were evacuated for days.
Sylmar's name, adopted in 1893, joins Latin words for forest and sea, for the sea of olive trees that covered these slopes.
In 1894 up to 1,700 acres were planted, and by 1906 the groves were said to be the largest olive grove in the world.
Today Sylmar is a suburb, the northernmost neighborhood in Los Angeles.
Near the freeway sits the Sylmar Converter Station, the south end of the Pacific DC Intertie, a power line that runs 846 miles from the Columbia River near The Dalles, Oregon.
The line carries direct current, and this station turns it into the alternating current Los Angeles uses, up to 3,100 megawatts.
On the hillside beside the freeway, water from the eastern Sierra Nevada tumbles down the Cascades, the end of the Los Angeles Aqueduct.
When the first water arrived on November 5, 1913, chief engineer William Mulholland said, "There it is.
The original aqueduct runs 233 miles and moves its water by gravity alone.
This tangle of ramps, where I-5 meets the Antelope Valley Freeway, is the Newhall Pass interchange, and parts of I-5 here are up to 21 lanes wide.
Earthquakes knocked down ramps here twice, in 1971 and again in 1994.
Officially it is the Clarence Wayne Dean Memorial Interchange, named for a police officer killed in the 1994 collapse.
In Placerita Canyon, a few miles east, Francisco López made what the state's landmark plaque calls California's first authenticated gold discovery, on March 9, 1842.
Gathering wild onions near an oak tree, he found gold flakes clinging to the onion roots.
That was six years before the famous strike at Sutter's Mill, and the tree is now called the Oak of the Golden Dream.
Before tunnels and freeways, stagecoaches crossed this pass through Beale's Cut, a slot dug through the mountain with picks and shovels and eventually deepened to 90 feet.
Edward Beale, who won the right to collect tolls here in 1863, used Chinese immigrant workers to do most of the digging.
Butterfield Overland Mail coaches running to San Francisco used the cut.
In Newhall, the ranch of silent film cowboy William S. Hart is now a 265-acre park with his Spanish-style mansion, trails and a barnyard of farm animals.
Hart left it to Los Angeles County when he died in 1946.
Before he died he said, "When I was making pictures, the people gave me their nickels, dimes, and quarters.
When I am gone, I want them to have my home."
Up Pico Canyon, west of the freeway, Well Number 4 struck oil on September 26, 1876, and became the first commercially successful oil well in the western United States.
It kept producing for 114 years until it was capped in 1990, and it is often called the longest continuously operating oil well in the world.
The Santa Clarita Valley is considered the heart of the homeland of the Tataviam people, a name that means people on the south slope in the neighboring Kitanemuk language.
They lived in about 20 villages in and around the valley, with summer and winter settlements, and harvested yucca and juniper berries.
Their tribe today, the Fernandeño Tataviam Band of Mission Indians, is governed from San Fernando.
The Santa Clara River, which passes under the freeway near Magic Mountain Parkway, runs 83 miles to the Pacific and is one of the least altered rivers in Southern California.
Here its bed is dry most of the year.

Spanish explorers named it on August 9, 1769, for Saint Clare of Assisi, and the valley later became known as little Santa Clara, Santa Clarita, to tell it apart from Santa Clara in Northern California.
The roller coaster tracks twisting over the hills west of the freeway belong to Six Flags Magic Mountain, which opened on May 29, 1971.
In 2022 it became the first amusement park to offer 20 roller coasters.
Several have closed since, but it still has one of the biggest collections of coasters anywhere.
Near where Highway 126 meets the freeway stood the adobe headquarters of Rancho San Francisco, first built about 1804 as a granary for Mission San Fernando.

In January 1850, William Lewis Manly and John Rogers reached it and got supplies and animals to rescue their gold-seeking emigrant party, stranded and starving in Death Valley about 250 miles northeast.
Just before midnight on March 12, 1928, the St. Francis Dam failed in San Francisquito Canyon, about 10 miles north of Santa Clarita.
The flood tore down the canyon and along the Santa Clara River to the sea, killing at least 431 people.
It is considered the second-deadliest dam failure in American history.
Val Verde, the Black Palm Springs.
In the hills west of the freeway, Black investors led by Sidney Dones founded a resort community in 1924, when African Americans were often barred from public beaches and pools.
It became known as the Black Palm Springs, and Ella Fitzgerald and Lena Horne appeared there.
Today it is the community of Val Verde, Spanish for green valley.
On the Five Mile Grade north of Castaic, the two sides of the freeway trade places, so for about 5 miles traffic keeps to the left.
When I-5 was rebuilt in the 1960s, engineers put the uphill and downhill lanes on separate hillsides, and the downhill lanes got a gentler grade to cut down on runaway trucks.
Castaic takes its name from the Chumash word Kaštiq, meaning the eye.
Above the town, Castaic Dam, finished in 1973, rises 340 feet and stretches nearly a mile, holding Castaic Lake at the end of the West Branch of the California Aqueduct.
Water from Northern California rests here before flowing on to millions of people around Los Angeles.
East of the freeway, the original Ridge Route of 1915 winds along the ridgetops from Castaic toward Gorman.
It was the first paved highway linking Los Angeles directly with the San Joaquin Valley, and between Castaic and Gorman its 697 turns added up to about 97 complete circles in 36 miles.
Between Castaic and Quail Lake the speed limit was 15 miles an hour.
Beneath Pyramid Lake lies a drowned highway.
In 1933 the three-lane Ridge Route Alternate, later US 99, opened through the canyon of Piru Creek, with a middle lane that drivers in both directions used for passing, nicknamed the suicide lane.
After Pyramid Dam was finished, rising water covered the old road, and by 1972 it was fully under the lake.
The Vista del Lago Visitors Center, off its own exit, sits above Pyramid Lake with an outdoor overlook and exhibits from the California Department of Water Resources.
The lake holds about 180,000 acre-feet of State Water Project water, pumped up from the San Joaquin Valley and over the Tehachapi Mountains.
Quail Lake, along Highway 138 east of the freeway, lies in the rift zone of the San Andreas Fault and stores water for the West Branch of the California Aqueduct.
Water pumped up to the lake flows by gravity through a pipeline to a power plant at Pyramid Lake.
The fault itself slices right through Gorman.
In spring after a wet winter, California poppies and lupine can blanket the hills around Gorman.
People have stopped here for centuries:
it was the Tataviam village of Kulshra'jek, a trading crossroads, and a local historian calls it one of the oldest continuously used roadside rest stops in California.
Near the top of Tejon Pass, I-5 reaches 4,144 feet, its highest point in California, close to the line between Los Angeles and Kern counties.
The pass sits where California's two largest faults, the San Andreas and the Garlock, meet.
Tejón is Spanish for badger, though the dead badger behind the name was found in 1806 at a different canyon, about 15 miles northeast.
At 2 in the morning on July 11, 2022, a Brink's tractor-trailer carrying jewelry from a show in San Mateo to one in Pasadena pulled into a truck stop at the Frazier Mountain Park Road exit.
One guard went inside to eat while the other slept in the cab.
Within 27 minutes, thieves cut the trailer's padlock and made off with about two dozen of its 73 bags of jewelry.
The broad, pine-covered peak west of the pass is Frazier Mountain, 8,017 feet high.
To the Chumash people it is Toshololo, the mountain of the east, named for its place east of Mount Pinos and tied to the morning star and the spring equinox.
Its English name honors William Frazer, a miner who worked here in the 1850s.
The open hills around Lebec are part of Tejon Ranch, more than 270,000 acres and the largest single piece of private land in California.
Cattle graze about 250,000 acres of it, up to 12,000 head depending on the season.
The ranch says you know winter is over when orange poppies spill across the hills and young calves trail their mothers.
East of Lebec lies Castac Lake, a natural salty lake that formed about 10,000 years ago when the fan of sediment washed down by Cuddy Creek dammed a valley along the Garlock Fault.
The Chumash, Kitanemuk and Yokuts peoples all named it for an eye.
The adobe buildings among the oaks beside the freeway are Fort Tejon, an Army post from 1854 to 1864 on the main route between the Central Valley and Southern California.
From 1858 it was the western end of the Army's experiment with camels as pack animals.
The soldiers found the camels hardy but temperamental, and they spooked the cavalry's horses.
On the fort grounds is the grave of Peter Lebeck, buried under a valley oak in 1837.
Someone carved his epitaph into the tree:
Peter Lebeck, killed by a X bear, October 17, 1837.
Early settlers called grizzlies X bears, probably for a dark pattern on their backs, and he is the earliest known victim of a bear attack in California.
This steep stretch through Grapevine Canyon is the Grapevine itself, a 6 percent grade that runs 5 miles and drops about 1,600 feet.
Escape ramps branch off the downhill lanes for big rigs whose brakes fail, and in hot weather car engines often overheat on the long uphill lanes.
These mountains are ancestral homeland of the Tejon Indian Tribe, a federally recognized tribe of Kitanemuk, Yokuts, Paiute and Chumash people based in Bakersfield.
In 1853 they became the site of California's first Indian reservation, the Sebastian, or Tejon, Reservation, which reached from Tejon Canyon west to Grapevine Canyon.
The state's historical marker says the number of people living there varied from 500 to 2,000.
About 6 miles east of here, the Edmonston Pumping Plant lifts California Aqueduct water 1,926 feet up and over the Tehachapi Mountains toward Southern California.
Apart from pumped-storage power plants, it is the most powerful water-lifting system in the world.
At full capacity its pumps can send nearly 2 million gallons a minute uphill.
At the foot of the Grapevine, the freeway reaches the southern tip of the San Joaquin Valley, about 1,500 feet above sea level.
Between Tejon Pass and here, the road changes elevation by more than 2,600 feet in about 12 miles.
From here the Central Valley, broad and flat, runs about 450 miles between the Coast Ranges and the Sierra Nevada.
The long, low ridge where the mountains meet the valley floor here is Wheeler Ridge, a fold in the earth's crust that is still growing.
It is being pushed up over a thrust fault, and geologists have found that the fold is getting longer at its eastern end, toward the east-southeast.
At 4:52 in the morning on July 21, 1952, the White Wolf Fault broke near Wheeler Ridge in a magnitude 7.3 earthquake, the strongest in California since 1906.
It killed 12 people, and the mountain town of Tehachapi was hit hardest.
Out in the valley fields, rows of cotton were found shifted sideways, one of them by 3 feet.
Start of the West Side Freeway.
Highway 99 and I-5 meet at the Wheeler Ridge interchange.
From here to Woodland, I-5 is the West Side Freeway.
It was chosen as the Interstate route because it skips the valley's big cities, such as Bakersfield and Fresno, for a faster, more direct trip.
The section between here and Los Banos opened in 1972.

On September 30, 1955, the actor James Dean was driving north on Highway 99, on his way to a sports car race in Salinas, when a Highway Patrol officer pulled him over near here and wrote him a speeding ticket.
The officer listed the place as Mettler Station.
Later that same day, Dean was killed in a crash farther along his trip.

In the hills southwest of here lies Wind Wolves Preserve, 93,000 acres of grassland, oak and canyon that its owner, The Wildlands Conservancy, calls the largest nonprofit nature preserve on the West Coast.
The name describes tall grass bending and parting in gusts of wind, like unseen animals running across the slopes.
In 1998, 19 tule elk were released here, and the herd has grown to about 500.
Near Maricopa, in March 1910, an oil well called Lakeview Number One blew out and would not stop.
For 18 months it gushed, about 9 million barrels in all, and it is often called the largest accidental oil spill in history.
The force of the flow destroyed the derrick.
The mountains forming the valley's southern wall are the San Emigdio Mountains, which top out at 7,492 feet.
They are named for Saint Emygdius, an early Christian martyr whom Catholics call on for protection from earthquakes.
The flat fields near the freeway here were once Kern Lake, the smallest of three big lakes at the south end of the valley.
It was the first lake the Kern River fed.
From Kern Lake, water ran west through a channel called Connecting Slough into Buena Vista Lake, and in wet years the two joined into one large lake.
Diverting the river for farms in the 1800s left it a dry bed.
Many of the neat rows of trees in Kern County are almonds and pistachios.
In 2022 the county harvested about 223,000 acres of almonds and 158,000 acres of pistachios, more pistachio acres than any other county in California.
Together those two nuts were worth about 1.6 billion dollars that year, and California grows 99 percent of the country's pistachios.
Highway 119 leads to Taft, an oil town at the valley's southwest edge.

The town's oil museum tells how locals asked the railroad to name its station Moro, but the railroad worried it would be confused with Morro Bay and named it Moron instead, back when the word did not yet mean anything unkind.
In 1909 the town took a new name, for President William Howard Taft.
Southwest of here, much of the farmland was once Buena Vista Lake, fed by the Kern River and the second largest of the lakes in the Tulare Basin.
On its south shore stood Tulamniu, a Yokuts village lived in for several centuries, which the Spanish commander Pedro Fages named Buena Vista in 1772.
Two small lakes, Lake Webb and Lake Evans, now sit on part of the old bed.
The freeway crosses the Kern River here, though this far downstream its channel is often dry.
John C. Frémont named the river in 1845 for Edward Kern, the mapmaker of his expedition, who, as the story goes, nearly drowned in its rushing water.
Long before that, in 1776, the Spanish missionary Francisco Garcés had called it the Río de San Felipe.
Near here, the Kern Water Bank covers about 32 square miles of the southern San Joaquin Valley.
In wet years, water is spread into more than 80 basins and slowly soaks into the ground, where it is saved for dry years.
It can store 1.5 million acre-feet underground, more than two and a half times what Lake Isabella, the big reservoir upriver, can hold.
A few miles southwest, Tule Elk State Natural Reserve keeps a herd of about 30 to 35 tule elk on nearly 1,000 acres, watched from a viewing platform.
These elk are found only in California.
About half a million once roamed the state, but by the 1870s they were thought to be extinct, until a few were found hiding in the tules near Buena Vista Lake.
The low hills to the west are the Elk Hills, over one of the most productive oil fields in the country.
In 1912 President Taft made them the nation's first Naval Petroleum Reserve, oil saved for the Navy.
In 1922 Interior Secretary Albert Fall leased them, without competitive bidding, to oilman Edward Doheny, who had quietly lent Fall 100,000 dollars with no interest.
The deal became part of the Teapot Dome scandal.
Buttonwillow was a headquarters of Miller and Lux, the company of Henry Miller, known as the Cattle King of California.
Miller came west in 1850 as a butcher and teamed up with another German immigrant, Charles Lux, in 1858.
At its height the company owned about 1.4 million acres outright and controlled nearly 22,000 square miles of land in California, Nevada and Oregon.
The big electrical yard about a mile east of Buttonwillow is Midway Substation.
Here Southern California Edison's power lines, which cross the mountains to the south, meet PG&E's grid.
In winter, power often flows north toward the Pacific Northwest, where people run heaters; in summer it flows south for air conditioners.
The town of Buttonwillow is named for a single tree, and it is not a willow at all.
A lone one here stood out as a landmark on an old trail across the valley, and it was a Yokuts meeting place long before settlers held stock rodeos beside it.
The tree is now California Historical Landmark 492.
About 7 miles northeast of here lies the center of population of California.
The Census Bureau finds it by imagining a flat, weightless map of the state with every resident given the same weight, then finding the point where the map would balance.
Since 1970, that point has stayed within about 10 miles of Buttonwillow.
West of Buttonwillow, near the tiny town of McKittrick, natural asphalt oozes out of the ground from the oil field below.
Like the La Brea Tar Pits in Los Angeles, these pits trapped animals during the ice ages, from about 15,000 to 50,000 years ago.
Fossils found here include saber-toothed cats, short-faced bears, American lions, ground sloths, bison and mammoths.
Cotton has deep roots on this side of the valley.
Sandy loam soils, a long growing season without rain, big irrigation systems and relative freedom from pests like the boll weevil made the San Joaquin Valley ideal cotton land.
A strain called Acala, developed at the cotton research station in nearby Shafter, became so important that state laws passed in 1925 made it the only cotton allowed in key areas.
On clear days, the mountains along the far western skyline are the Temblor Range, named from the Spanish word for tremor.
The San Andreas Fault runs along the foot of their far side, at the edge of the Carrizo Plain.
The peaks average about 3,500 feet, and the highest, McKittrick Summit, reaches 4,331 feet.
This dry west side of the valley is home to the San Joaquin kit fox, an endangered fox with huge ears.
Kit foxes are the smallest wild members of the dog family in North America, and an adult weighs only about 5 pounds.
It hunts mostly at night, mainly for kangaroo rats.
A few miles west, the California Aqueduct flows downhill by gravity, with no pumps.
From the Coastal Branch split south of Kettleman City, its water runs about 66 miles to the Buena Vista Pumping Plant, the first of four plants that lift it toward and over the Tehachapi Mountains.
The canal is built on a slight grade so gravity does the work.
West on Highway 46, where it meets Highway 33, Blackwells Corner is named for George Blackwell, who started a rest stop there in 1921.
James Dean stopped there in 1955, and it is often described as the last place he was seen alive before his fatal crash near Cholame.
Lost Hills, a town of about 2,400 people a couple of miles west of the freeway, takes its name from the low Lost Hills range beside it.
Many residents work for the Wonderful Company, whose pistachio and almond processing plant is here.
Each fall, pistachio trees are shaken and the nuts hauled to processing plants; at the one in Lost Hills, workers sort them by hand.
In July 1910, two drillers named Martin and Dudley were drilling a water well for livestock in the low hills west of here.
At 530 feet they struck oil instead, and the Lost Hills oil field was born.
The hills rise barely 200 feet above the valley, and so much oil has been pumped out that parts of them have sunk as much as 8 feet.
From November through March, tule fog can fill this southern end of the valley.
The thick ground fog, named for the tule marshes of the Central Valley, tends to last longer in the south and east of the valley than farther north.
Inside it, visibility is usually less than 600 feet, and it can drop to almost nothing within a few feet.
East of here, Kern National Wildlife Refuge protects 11,249 acres of desert uplands, an old river corridor and marsh on the southern edge of what was once Tulare Lake.
In winter its wetlands shelter migrating ducks, geese and other water birds that travel the Pacific Flyway.
The line between Kern and Kings counties crosses the freeway here.
Kern County, formed in 1866, takes its name from the Kern River.
Kings County, carved out of Tulare County in 1893, takes its name from the Kings River, which Spanish soldiers called the River of the Holy Kings.
The soils of the San Joaquin Valley, especially its southern end, can hold Coccidioides, a fungus that causes valley fever, also called San Joaquin Valley fever.
Its spores rise into the air when dusty ground is stirred up by wind, farming or construction, and people catch it by breathing them in.
It is not contagious, and about 60 percent of people who are infected have few or no symptoms.
A few miles west of here, a branch of the California Aqueduct splits off and heads for the coast.
The Coastal Branch runs 116 miles, climbing through five pumping plants to deliver water to San Luis Obispo, Santa Maria and Santa Barbara.
Utica Avenue leads east to Alpaugh, a town on what was once Atwell's Island, the largest island in Tulare Lake.
It was first known as Hog-Root Island, and a Visalia lawyer named Allen Atwell raised hogs on it.
The island was a regular stop for the lake's commercial ferry.
About 30 miles east, past Alpaugh, Colonel Allensworth State Historic Park preserves the first California town founded, financed and governed by African Americans.
Army veteran Allen Allensworth and four partners started it in 1908, hoping to build a Tuskegee of the West, a place where Black families could own land, farm and run their own affairs.
The freeway crosses the California Aqueduct here, the concrete river that carries water from the Sacramento-San Joaquin Delta toward Southern California.
Counting from the south, this is the second of I-5's five crossings of the aqueduct.
A typical stretch is 40 feet wide at the bottom and holds water about 30 feet deep, and the whole aqueduct runs more than 400 miles.
East of here lies the bed of Tulare Lake, once the largest freshwater lake west of the Mississippi River.
The Tachi Yokut Tribe calls it Pa'ashi, big water.
The rivers that fed it were diverted for farming, and by 1899 it was dry except for marshes.
A landfill and a town's fight.

Off Highway 41, about 3.5 miles southwest of Kettleman City, the Kettleman Hills facility is a landfill of about 1,500 acres for hazardous and household waste, run by a subsidiary of Waste Management.
In recent decades it has been the focus of an environmental justice fight in Kettleman City, a small, mostly Spanish-speaking farmworker town.
Kettleman City is near the halfway point between Los Angeles and San Francisco or Sacramento, which makes this exit a major stop for food and lodging.
The travel stops cluster at the Highway 41 junction, while the town itself, about 1,200 people, sits about a mile north, past the aqueduct.
It lies only about half a mile north of the 36th parallel.
The long, low hills along the west side are the Kettleman Hills, about 30 miles long and up to about 1,200 feet high.
They are named, with a spelling change, for Dave Kettelman, who grazed sheep and cattle here in the 1860s.
They are a long fold in the rock, squeezed up by tectonic forces, and they run parallel to the San Andreas Fault, farther west.
In October 1928, after 19 months of drilling, the Milham Exploration Company's Elliott Number 1 well struck oil more than 7,000 feet under the Kettleman Hills.
It blew out with a roar heard 20 miles away, spraying oil so light that it was white, and it reportedly could run a car without refining.
The Kettleman North Dome became one of the most productive oil fields in the country.
Highway 269 crosses the Kettleman Hills to Avenal, whose name is Spanish for oat field.
Spanish soldiers and explorers named it for the wild oats, waist high, that covered the plain like golden silk.
Standard Oil laid out the town in 1929, after oil was found in the hills, and its first post office was a cigar box on the counter of the general store.
Fresno County grows most of the garlic in the United States, and west side towns such as Huron picked up the slack as Gilroy, once the country's biggest garlic producer, ran out of room.
In 2022 the county harvested about 23,000 acres and 185,000 tons of garlic, nearly two-thirds of California's crop, worth about 350 million dollars.
The sprawling electrical yard east of the freeway is Gates Substation, a key junction on the power lines linking Northern and Southern California.
Between here and Los Banos, the corridor once had only two of its biggest lines.
That bottleneck limited how much power could flow, and it was one of the leading causes of the California electricity crisis of 2000 and 2001.
East of the freeway is Huron, a farm town of about 6,200 people that swells to more than 15,000 at harvest time, when migrant farmworkers arrive.
It began in 1888 as a water stop on the Southern Pacific Railroad.
In the 2000 census, Huron had the highest share of Hispanic or Latino residents of any city in the United States.
The freeway bridges here cross Los Gatos Creek, once called Arroyo Pasajero, the travelers' creek.
On March 10, 1995, extreme rain sent fast floodwater down the creek.
The flood scoured the creek bed and undermined the bridge piers, both I-5 bridges failed, and four cars and a truck went into the creek.
The Harris Ranch restaurant opened beside the freeway in 1977, aimed at local farmers, and soon became a popular stop for travelers on the busy freeway between Los Angeles and San Francisco.
A 153-room hacienda-style inn was added in 1987, and by 2008 the restaurant ranked sixth in California by sales.
The long, low ridge between the freeway and Coalinga is Anticline Ridge, part of the Coalinga Oil Field, one of only six California fields to have produced more than a billion barrels of oil.
By 1910 it was the most productive oil field in the state.
Long before drillers came, Native people here used tar from natural seeps to line baskets and to trade.
Coalinga began in 1888 as a Southern Pacific coaling stop for steam locomotives.
The railroad called it Coaling Station A. Local tradition says a railroad official made the name more musical by adding an a.
It is just as likely that a small station sign squeezed Coaling A into Coalinga.
At 4:42 on the afternoon of May 2, 1983, a magnitude 6.2 earthquake struck Coalinga.
The town's eight-block downtown was almost destroyed, with the worst damage to buildings with unreinforced brick walls, and 94 people were injured.
The shaking was felt from the Los Angeles area to Susanville, in Lassen County.
Harris Ranch is California's largest beef producer, and its feedlot sits right beside the freeway.
It holds more than 100,000 cattle on more than 800 acres, so many travelers notice it by smell first.
That smell inspired food writer Michael Pollan's research on factory farming, which led to his book The Omnivore's Dilemma.
Much of the west side of Fresno and Kings counties, along this part of the freeway, is served by Westlands Water District, formed in 1952.
By irrigable acres it is the largest farm water district in the country, about 614,000 acres, where roughly 700 farmers own land.
On January 28, 1948, a chartered DC-3 crashed in the Diablo Range about 20 miles west of Coalinga, near Los Gatos Creek.
Most were Mexican farmworkers being sent back to Mexico, some at the end of their bracero contracts.
First news reports named only the pilot, copilot, flight attendant and immigration guard, and listed the rest simply as deportees.
On the high ridge west of the freeway stand three stone pillars, about 4,100 feet up.
These are the Joaquin Rocks, once called Las Tres Piedras, the Three Rocks, and they can be seen for miles across the valley.
They are named for the Gold Rush bandit Joaquin Murrieta, whose gang is said to have used them as a lookout.
Where Cantua Creek leaves the hills, about a mile and a half west of the freeway, is Arroyo de Cantua, said to be the hideout of the Gold Rush bandit Joaquin Murrieta.
On July 25, 1853, California Rangers led by Captain Harry Love attacked a band of armed Mexican men near here, killed three, and claimed one of them was Murrieta.
Highway 33 leads from here to Mendota, known as the Cantaloupe Center of the World.
It began to thrive in 1891 as a Southern Pacific storage and switching yard, and the railroad borrowed its name from Mendota, Illinois.
The town sits beside the San Joaquin River, near where the Delta-Mendota Canal pours in water to refill a riverbed that is often dry.
Fresno County, which the freeway crosses here, was the number one farm county in the nation in 2017, when its crops and livestock were worth almost 8 billion dollars.
About 1.9 million acres, nearly half the county, are farmed.
More than 300 crops grow here, and the leaders range from grapes, pistachios and almonds to tomatoes, cotton and milk.
Starting around 2008, big signs went up in fields along I-5, with slogans like Congress Created Dust Bowl and No Water Equals No Jobs.
Many came from Families Protecting the Valley, a loosely organized group of San Joaquin Valley farmers and other locals.
Russ Waymire, a Hanford real estate broker and former farmer, put up its first sign with a friend's help, and farmers soon offered their land for more.
On November 29, 1991, the Friday after Thanksgiving, a sudden dust storm swept this stretch of I-5 north of Coalinga and dropped visibility to near zero.
In a series of chain-reaction crashes, 104 vehicles collided, 17 people died and 150 were hurt.
The Highway Patrol called it the deadliest dust storm crash in state history.
The mountains west of the freeway are the Diablo Range, part of California's Coast Ranges.
It stretches from the Carquinez Strait, near the Bay Area, south to Polonio Pass, near Cholame.
Its highest point, San Benito Mountain, rises to 5,241 feet in remote country to the southwest.
Long before the freeway, an older road ran along this side of the valley:
El Camino Viejo, the Old Road to Los Angeles, the oldest north-south trail in the interior of Spanish and Mexican California.
Spanish ox carts used it as early as 1780, traveling from one creek or waterhole to the next along the foot of the Coast Ranges, between San Pedro Bay and the shore of San Francisco Bay at Oakland.
Southwest of Mendota, east of the freeway, the ground sank about 28 feet between 1925 and 1977 because so much groundwater was pumped from under the fields.
A famous photo shows U.S. Geological Survey scientist Joseph Poland beside a utility pole there, with signs high on the pole marking where the ground surface was in 1925 and 1955.
The low hills west of the freeway are the Panoche Hills, rising east of the higher Diablo Range.
Their name is thought to come from a local Native word for a cane that once grew in the valley beyond them, from which people made panoche, a kind of sugar.
Panoche Creek and the mercury mines.
Panoche Creek, which comes out of the hills near here, drains a larger area than any other stream on the Diablo Range's eastern slope.
Its old Spanish name was Arroyo de Panoche Grande, Big Sugarloaf Creek.
It was part of a route between Native settlements on the central coast and the valley, and a watering place on El Camino Viejo.
On Little Panoche Road, in the hills west of the freeway, Mercey Hot Springs has been a resort since the early 1900s.
Water flows from one spring at 119 degrees Fahrenheit, and the resort has cabins, campsites, bathtub soaking pools and a swimming pool fed by a hot artesian well.
The big canal on this part of the drive is officially the San Luis Canal, the federally built section of the California Aqueduct.

It carries water for both the state and federal water projects from O'Neill Forebay to Kettleman City, and with room for 13,100 cubic feet of water a second, it is one of the largest irrigation canals in the country.
East of the freeway, on the San Joaquin River, is Firebaugh, named for Andrew Firebaugh, a Virginian who ran a ferry across the river during the Gold Rush.
The settlement, then called Firebaugh's Ferry, became a station on the Butterfield Overland stage line.
A water tank in its small downtown is painted with the city's name.
Caltrans rebuilt both sides of the John Chuck Erreca Rest Area in a 30 million dollar project, reopening one side in August 2025 and the other in May 2026.
Caltrans calls it one of the most sustainable rest areas it has ever built, with utilities designed to use little water and power.
East of the freeway, the San Joaquin River winds past Firebaugh.
The southern Yokuts name for it, Tihshachu, means salmon-spearing place.
Its Spanish name dates to explorer Gabriel Moraga, who named one of its branches for Saint Joachim between 1805 and 1808, and the name was in common use by 1810.
Beside the freeway, the Dos Amigos Pumping Plant lifts California Aqueduct water 118 feet.

Its six pumps can move 15,450 cubic feet of water a second, and that single boost lets the water flow by gravity for about 95 miles, to where the aqueduct's Coastal Branch splits off south of Kettleman City.
East of the freeway lie the Grasslands, about 250 square miles of wetlands and grasslands along the San Joaquin River, named a wetland of international importance under the Ramsar treaty.
They sit on the Pacific Flyway, the great bird migration route, and are important habitat for resident and migrating water birds.
Path 15, part of California's main north-south power corridor, runs along this side of the valley, generally 3 to 7 miles west of the freeway.
Its 500,000-volt lines run from the Los Banos substation, west of Los Banos, to Midway, near Buttonwillow, linking hydroelectric plants in the north with fossil fuel power plants in the south.
Los Banos, the city about 7 miles east of the freeway, is Spanish for the baths.
It is named for pools known as the baths of Padre Arroyo, a regular stop for priests from Mission San Juan Bautista on trips into the valley, visited by Spanish explorers as early as 1805.
Later settlers called the stream Los Banos Creek, and the post office and town took the name too.
The Morning Star Company, which opened its first tomato factory in Los Banos in 1990 and another at Santa Nella in 2002, was the world's leading tomato processor as of 2023.
It handles about 5 million tons of tomatoes a year, roughly 40 percent of California's processing tomato crop, for products like tomato paste and diced tomatoes.
Tule elk at San Luis refuge.
About 13 miles east, San Luis National Wildlife Refuge, established in 1967, keeps a herd of reintroduced tule elk, the smallest kind of elk.
Its more than 26,800 acres of wetlands, riverside woods, native grasslands and vernal pools are also a major wintering ground and stopover for waterfowl and shorebirds on the Pacific Flyway.
Highway 152 heads west over Pacheco Pass, at 1,368 feet the main route through the hills between the Central Valley and the Santa Clara Valley.
Yokuts people used a trail nearby to cross the mountains and trade with Native people on the coast, and Spanish officer Gabriel Moraga first recorded the pass in 1805.
West of the freeway, B.F. Sisk Dam, 382 feet high and more than three and a half miles long, holds back San Luis Reservoir, the largest offstream reservoir in the nation.
Most of its water does not flow in from a river at all:
it is pumped in from canals fed by the Delta and stored for the dry months.
Santa Nella sounds like a saint's name, but there is no Saint Nella.
The name is an English mangling of the Spanish word centinela, sentinel, from Rancho de Centinela, a horse ranch started here in 1810 by stockmen from San Juan Bautista and Monterey.
Pea Soup Andersen's opened here in 1976 as the second location of a roadside restaurant famous for its pea soup.
When the 1924 original in Buellton closed in January 2024, just before its 100th anniversary, this became the only Pea Soup Andersen's left.
Its working windmill can be seen from the freeway.
West of the freeway, on McCabe Road near Santa Nella, is San Joaquin Valley National Cemetery, on land the Romero Ranch Company donated in 1989.
It covers 322 acres, its first section was finished in 1992, and more than 30,000 burials had taken place there by 2008.
Two big canals run side by side along the western edge of the valley between here and Tracy:
the state's California Aqueduct and the federal Delta-Mendota Canal.
The Delta-Mendota, finished in 1951, starts at a pumping plant near Tracy that lifts water 197 feet out of the Delta, and it runs 117 miles to the San Joaquin River near Mendota.
About 11 miles east is Kesterson Reservoir, now part of San Luis National Wildlife Refuge.
In 1983 scientists found that 64 percent of the water bird embryos and hatchlings there were deformed or dead, poisoned by selenium in farm drainage water.
The discovery drew national attention, and the ponds were closed in 1986.
The town of Gustine, east of the freeway, is named for Sara Miller, the daughter of cattle king Henry Miller.
Her middle name was Augustine and her nickname was Gussie, and she died at eight after being thrown from her horse.
Gustine grew up in the early 1900s as a Southern Pacific station, opened its post office in 1907 and became a city in 1915.
About 7 miles east, where the Merced River meets the San Joaquin, stood Hills Ferry, a river crossing started in 1850 and taken over by Jesse Hill in 1854.
By the late 1870s it was a busy grain shipping town of several hundred people.
When the railroad came through Newman in 1888, Hills Ferry quickly faded away.
The town of Newman, east of the freeway, was founded in 1888 by Simon Newman, a businessman who came to California from Bavaria as a teenager in 1862.
Born Simon Neumann, he arrived speaking only German and Hebrew, learned English, and translated his family name.
Almonds are the top farm product of Stanislaus County, which the freeway crosses here.
Each February, the pollination of California's almonds is the largest managed pollination event in the world:
more than a million beehives, nearly half of all the hives in the country, are trucked in to the orchards.
East of the freeway is the old Crows Landing airfield.
The Navy broke ground on December 1, 1942, and trained pilots here in Wildcat and Avenger warplanes during World War Two, later adding big patrol bombers.
NASA's Ames Research Center took it over in 1993, and in 2022 the county announced plans to turn it into a business park.

Thomas Patterson wanted his town to look different from other farm towns, so he laid it out like Washington, D.C., and Paris, with circles and streets spreading out like spokes, and its main streets were planted with palms, eucalyptus and sycamores.
In 1971 its chamber of commerce named Patterson the Apricot Capital of the World.
Diablo Grande Parkway leads into the Diablo Range to Diablo Grande, a gated hillside community about 9 miles southwest of Patterson, at 1,535 feet.
Developer Donald Panoz dreamed of a resort town with up to 10,000 homes, six golf courses, a resort hotel and spa, vineyards and a winery.
West of Patterson, Del Puerto Canyon cuts into the Diablo Range.
Spanish travelers called its creek Arroyo de La Puerta, the Creek of the Door, for the narrow gap where it squeezes out of the canyon into the valley.
This is the homeland of the Hoyumne and Miumne, Northern Valley Yokuts peoples, who left grinding rocks and a path carved into the Gateway rocks at the canyon's mouth.
In August 2020 a cluster of wildfires burned through the Diablo Range west of the freeway.
The SCU Lightning Complex burned nearly 400,000 acres, more than 600 square miles, across six counties between August 16 and October 1, one of the largest wildfires in modern California history.
On September 22, 1999, lightning struck a huge pile of about six million old tires near Westley.
The fire burned for 34 days, and the melting rubber turned into at least 250,000 gallons of oil.
Cleanup was estimated to cost more than 20 million dollars.
On clear days a lone, double-peaked mountain stands on the northwest skyline:
Mount Diablo, 3,849 feet tall and about 40 miles away.
In 1851 Colonel Leander Ransom chose its south peak as the starting point for land surveys, and land in most of Northern California and all of Nevada is still described from it.
At this junction, I-580 heads for the Bay Area over Altamont Pass, a major crossing of the Diablo Range.
In all, I-580 runs about 76 miles, from San Rafael through Oakland to this meeting with I-5 south of Tracy.
Together with I-5, it is a main route between the Bay Area and Southern California.
Highway 33 leads to Vernalis, east of the freeway, whose name is Latin for springlike.
Local historian Earle Williams said it was named after two ranchers' daughters, Verna Carpenter and Alice Hamilton.
Its post office began in 1851 at nearby San Joaquin City and moved here in 1888.

East of the freeway, where the Tuolumne and Stanislaus rivers join the San Joaquin, San Joaquin River National Wildlife Refuge protects more than 7,000 acres of river woodland, wetlands and grassland.
It was set up in 1987 to protect the winter home of the Aleutian cackling goose, then endangered, and it has played a major part in the bird's recovery.
A few miles east, the Stanislaus River flows into the San Joaquin.
The river is named for Estanislao, the baptized name of Cucunuchi, a leader of the Lakisamni, a Yokuts people, and a Native official at Mission San Jose.
In the late 1820s he left the mission with about 400 followers and led raids on missions and settlers, until a Mexican army under Mariano Vallejo drove his people from the river in 1829.
West of the freeway is Banta, a settlement dating to the 1840s.
In stagecoach days it was the last stop before Altamont Pass on the road between Stockton and the Bay Area.
Henry Banta bought its inn in 1863 and changed the sign to read Banta's White House, and travelers soon called the whole place Bantas.
Tracy, west of the freeway, was born on September 8, 1878, when a Southern Pacific line from Oakland was joined to the Central Pacific line there, east of Altamont Pass.
The Tracy Historical Museum says the junction was named for Lathrop J. Tracy, a railroad executive from back east.
San Joaquin County, which the freeway crosses here, is a major national center of farming.
In its 2024 crop report, milk was the top commodity and almonds came second, with walnuts fifth and cherries sixth.
The county also has more acres of wine grapes than any other county in California.
The freeway crosses the San Joaquin River here, near a steel railroad lift bridge.

The first railroad bridge at this spot opened on September 6, 1869, and that afternoon the first through train from Sacramento crossed it, reaching Alameda by evening, where a ferry waited for San Francisco.
It was the last link of the first transcontinental railroad to the Pacific.
Manteca, a dairy town named lard.
Highway 120 leads east to Manteca, whose name is Spanish for lard.
That is an odd name for a town whose railroad stop was there to ship dairy products, and nobody agrees on how it happened.
One story says locals wanted a word for butter and the railroad got it wrong.
The authors of a county history think the Southern Pacific simply liked giving its stops appealing Spanish names.
Lathrop exists because of a quarrel.

When Stockton dragged its feet on where the railroad should run, Central Pacific president Leland Stanford built the line around the city and started a new town here, at a depot called Wilson's Station.
In 1869 it was renamed for the family of his wife, Jane Lathrop Stanford, and her brother Charles, an engineer for the railroad.
The Roth Road exit is signed for Sharpe Depot, an Army supply base.
In 1972 it became a hiding place for Flying Scotsman, often called the world's most famous steam locomotive.
Its owner had gone bankrupt touring it across North America, so he stored the engine at the Army depot here, out of reach of his creditors.
French Camp is considered the oldest settlement in San Joaquin County.
From about 1832 to 1845, French Canadian trappers working for the Hudson's Bay Company camped here every year with their families.
It was the southernmost regular camp of fur brigades sent all the way from Fort Vancouver, in what is now Vancouver, Washington.
The place was also called Castoria, from castor, the Latin word for beaver.
About a mile east of the freeway, on South Grant Street, is the first Sikh house of worship in the United States.
Gurdwara Sahib Stockton opened on October 24, 1912, in a house.
Its founders were Punjabi Sikh immigrants who farmed the land around Stockton.
Highway 4 heads east from here on the Crosstown Freeway, built in the early 1970s through part of Little Manila.
By 1946 this downtown neighborhood, south of Main Street, held the largest Filipino community in the United States.
Residents fought the freeway and lost, and it displaced many Filipino homes and businesses.
When Charles Weber laid out a town here in 1849, he called it Tuleburg.
He soon renamed it for Commodore Robert Stockton, a famed naval commander of the Mexican-American War.
That made Stockton the first town in California with a name that was neither Spanish nor Native American.
As the head of navigation on the San Joaquin River, it boomed as a supply stop for gold miners.
The docks just west of the freeway belong to the Port of Stockton, a seaport more than 70 nautical miles from the ocean.
Ocean ships up to 900 feet long come up a dredged channel, 35 feet deep, from San Francisco Bay.
The modern port opened on February 2, 1933, when the ship Daisy Grey arrived with a load of lumber from Oregon.
About a mile and a half east of the freeway is the University of the Pacific.
It was the first university chartered in California, in 1851, and it started out in Santa Clara.
It moved to San Jose in 1871 and to Stockton in 1924.
The freeway crosses the Calaveras River here.
The river is said to have been named in 1806 by the Spanish explorer Gabriel Moraga, when he found many skulls of Native people along its banks.
The Benjamin Holt Drive exit shares its name with a Stockton inventor.
On Thanksgiving Day, November 24, 1904, Holt tested a tractor that rode on tracks instead of wheels, plowing soggy Delta farmland near Stockton.
A company photographer was reported to have said it crawled like a caterpillar.
Caterpillar it is, he said, and the name lives on in the company Caterpillar Inc.
A 4.6-mile stretch of freeway north of Stockton was the very last piece of Interstate 5 to open.

On October 12, 1979, after 26 years of construction, the consuls of Canada and Mexico joined California's transportation secretary to cut a gold-colored chain, completing Interstate 5 from the Mexican border to the Canadian border.
Highway 12 leads east to Lodi, a town surrounded by vineyards.
Its growers raise more than 130 grape varieties, and many of the old vines here were planted between the Gold Rush and Prohibition.
Lodi is also the birthplace of A&W Root Beer:
in 1919 Roy Allen sold his first batch from a cart during a parade, and a plaque marks the spot.
From about 1900 through the 1970s, asparagus was a signature crop of the Delta west of here.
The first commercial crop was grown in 1892 on Bouldin Island by Chinese farmers.
