Every spear was cut by hand, with a long knife slipped just below the surface of the sticky peat soil, and crews walked each field every few days during the spring harvest.
A couple of miles west of the freeway, off Woodbridge Road, is the 353-acre Woodbridge Ecological Reserve, also called the Isenberg Sandhill Crane Reserve.
Sandhill cranes arrive in the Delta around late September and spend the fall and winter here.
Sunset is the best time to watch them fly in, giving a loud, trumpeting call that can be heard from a long way off.
West of the freeway lies the Sacramento-San Joaquin Delta, about 57 reclaimed islands and tracts ringed by 1,100 miles of levees.
Once the marsh was drained, its peat soil met the air and slowly broke down, and the land has sunk as much as 25 feet since the late 1800s.
Much of the western and central Delta now sits at least 15 feet below sea level.
Mokelumne, People of the Fish Net.
The freeway crosses the Mokelumne River here, about half a mile below the spot where the Cosumnes River flows into it.
Mokelumne joins moke, a fishnet, with umne, people of, so it means People of the Fish Net.
Cosumnes is thought to be built the same way, from kosum, salmon.

The Cosumnes River Preserve, whose visitor center is just east of the freeway, covers nearly 50,000 acres, including some of the largest remaining wetlands and streamside habitat in the Central Valley.
The Cosumnes is one of very few rivers on the western slope of the Sierra Nevada without a major dam, so it still floods over its banks in season, creating important habitat for wintering birds.
About three miles west of the freeway, on the Sacramento River levee a mile north of Walnut Grove, is Locke, the last of the Sacramento River Chinatowns to be built.
Immigrants from Heungshan County, in Guangdong, built it up after a 1915 fire destroyed the Chinese community in Walnut Grove.
California's Alien Land Law barred them from owning land, so they leased about nine acres from George Locke and owned only their buildings.
The freeway runs along the eastern edge of Stone Lakes National Wildlife Refuge, set aside in 1994.
It holds seasonal and permanent wetlands, grasslands, streamside forest and some of the last remaining freshwater lakes in the Central Valley.
It lies in the Delta, the destination of thousands of migrating waterfowl, shorebirds and other water birds.
Elk Grove Boulevard leads east into Elk Grove, which began in 1850 as a stagecoach stop for travelers between Sacramento and the Bay Area, when James Hall opened the Elk Grove Hotel.
Hall is said to have named it for elk antlers he found in the groves nearby, though he had also lived in a Missouri town with the same name.
Freeport, a town born of taxes.
The tiny river town of Freeport, just west of the freeway, began as a way around Sacramento's port taxes.
In 1862, businessmen tired of paying taxes at Sacramento's riverfront landing formed the Freeport Railroad Company to build a new port, free of those taxes, with a railroad that bypassed Sacramento.
The town boomed for three years and reached 300 to 400 people.
The Sutterville Road exit leads to William Land Park and the Sacramento Zoo, a few blocks east of the freeway.
The zoo opened on June 2, 1927, as the William Land Park Zoo, with 40 animals gathered from local parks, among them monkeys, raccoons, birds and deer.
Sacramento has been California's capital since 1854.
The new state's lawmakers first met in San Jose, moved to Vallejo in 1852 and to Benicia in 1853, and then settled here.
The State Capitol downtown, less than a mile east of the freeway, was modeled on the U.S. Capitol.
It was begun in 1860 and finished in 1874, and lawmakers moved into its chambers in 1869 while work went on around them.
The gold towers just west of the freeway belong to the Tower Bridge, a lift bridge over the Sacramento River dedicated in 1935.
Its 160-foot towers hold counterweights as heavy as the 1,150-ton middle span, so just two 100-horsepower electric motors can raise it to let tall boats through.
Through downtown Sacramento, I-5 runs below the water table, close beside the Sacramento River.
Caltrans calls this stretch the Boat Section.
It was built below street level in the 1960s and 1970s so the freeway would stay out of view of downtown offices and shops, and pumps, drains and a retaining wall keep the river's seepage out.
The California State Railroad Museum, in Old Sacramento, holds 21 restored locomotives and railroad cars, some dating back to 1862.
Inside, a large mock-up recreates railroad construction high in the Sierra at Donner Pass around 1867.
It features the Central Pacific's first locomotive, the Gov. Stanford, which came to California in pieces by ship, around Cape Horn.
The freeway crosses the American River here, close to where it flows into the Sacramento.
The park at the meeting of the two rivers, Discovery Park, is designed to flood.
In winter high water it can end up underwater, taking pressure off the American River levees.
Just east of the Arena Boulevard exit stood ARCO Arena, home of the Sacramento Kings from 1988 to 2016.
Built for just 40 million dollars, it was the cheapest arena in the NBA and the smallest.
In 2013 it set a Guinness World Record for the loudest sports roar, at 126 decibels.
Airport and the big red rabbit.
Sacramento International Airport, just north of the freeway, opened on October 21, 1967, with a single 8,600-foot runway.
Inside Terminal B is one of its odder sights:
Leap, a 56-foot red rabbit by the artist Lawrence Argent, made to look as if it had jumped into the building from outside.
The freeway crosses the Sacramento River here, the line between Sacramento and Yolo counties, on the Elkhorn Bridge, built in 1969 and also called the Vietnam Servicemen Memorial Bridge.
The Sacramento is the largest river in California.
It flows about 400 miles from the Klamath Mountains to the Delta and drains some 26,500 square miles.
The Elkhorn Causeway here crosses the Yolo Bypass, a floodway 41 miles long and about 3 miles wide.
When the Sacramento River runs high, it spills over weirs into the bypass, which can carry about four times the river's own flow and turns into an inland sea.
That takes pressure off the levees and lowers the flood risk for Sacramento and Davis.
County Road 102 leads north to Knights Landing, on the Sacramento River.
Dr. William Knight, a physician from Baltimore, founded it in 1843 on a mound that had long been a meeting place for the Native people living around Cache Creek and the river.
It grew into a steamboat landing and a ferry crossing.
The big plant half a mile from the freeway is the Woodland tomato cannery.
Tomatoes have been processed and canned here since 1958, under owners including Contadina and Del Monte, and Pacific Coast Producers has run it since 2001.
It works in season, generally July through September, and handles about 495,000 tons of tomatoes a year.
Woodland is the county seat of Yolo County and calls itself the City of Trees, for the valley oaks planted around town.
In 1853 Henry Wyckoff built a store here called Yolo City.
Frank Freeman bought it in 1857, gave land to anyone who would clear it and build a home, and in 1859 suggested the name Woodland.
Highway 16 heads west past Esparto into the Capay Valley, which Cache Creek flows through.
The valley is the traditional home of Patwin, or southern Wintun, people, and today it is home to the Yocha Dehe Wintun Nation, a federally recognized Patwin tribe.
The tribe is headquartered in Brooks, in the valley, where it runs the Cache Creek Casino Resort.
The freeway crosses Cache Creek here.
Its name comes from Hudson's Bay Company fur trappers, who cached, or hid, their furs along the Sacramento River and its smaller streams.
They called this one Riviere la Cache.
One of their camps, which early settlers knew as French Camp, stood in an oak grove on the creek's north bank, about a mile east of the town of Yolo.
The little town of Yolo shares its name with the county, and the name comes from the Patwin language.
Nobody is quite sure of its source.
It may come from Yo-loy, said to mean a place abounding in rushes, from a village called Yodoi near Knights Landing, or from that village's chief, Yodo.
In the state's original 1850 law, the county was spelled Yola.
Some fields in this part of the valley grow sunflowers for planting seed, not for snacks.

California has historically produced about 95 percent of the hybrid sunflower seed planted in the United States, and a quarter of the world's supply, with seed fields in Yolo County and elsewhere in the Sacramento Valley.
Bees carry pollen between interplanted rows of male and female plants to make the hybrid seed.
The farm community of Zamora was once called Black's, after J. J. Black, who settled here in 1865.

When the Northern Railway built its line north from Woodland in the 1870s, Black donated a strip of land for a depot, and a little town grew up around the station, with a hotel, stores, a jail, blacksmith shops and six warehouses.
I-505, once I-5W. Interstate 505 meets I-5 here and runs south to I-80 at Vacaville.

It was first planned as part of I-5W, a western loop of Interstate 5 through the Bay Area, while the route through Sacramento was to be I-5E. The split numbering was dropped, and the western loop became parts of I-580, I-80 and I-505.
In the winter of 1853, a flood washed two settlers, Copp and Wilson, off their claims near the Sacramento River, and they moved up to higher ground here.
The following year a Yolo County postal worker named A. W. Dunnigan arrived and went into the hotel business with Henry Yarick.
Their inn was known simply as Dunnigan's, and the town took his name.
Watch the fields and tall trees along here for the yellow-billed magpie, a black-and-white bird with a bright yellow bill and a small patch of yellow skin around each eye.
It lives only in California, in the Central Valley and the foothills and mountains beside it.
In good light its black feathers shine green, blue or purple.
About two miles east is College City, home to about 290 people and no college at all.
The town began with a school, Pierce Christian College, paid for with money from the estate of Andrew Pierce.
The college opened in 1875 and left town in 1896.
Arbuckle was laid out in 1875 and named for Tacitus Arbuckle, on whose ranch it grew.
To get a town going, he gave lots to anyone who would build on them, and he became its first postmaster.
The first train pulled in on July 4, 1876, just two months after the depot was finished.
The long, straight rows of trees around here are mostly almond orchards.
In 2024 almonds were Colusa County's most valuable crop, worth about 279 million dollars, from roughly 63,000 acres.
Almond pollination season usually runs from about mid-February to mid-March, when the trees bloom with fragrant white to pale pink flowers before their leaves come out.
On clear days, the cluster of peaks rising from the valley to the east is the Sutter Buttes, centered about 17 miles away.
They are the worn remains of a volcano that was active roughly a million and a half years ago, and they are often called the world's smallest mountain range.
The Maidu, Nisenan and Wintun names for them all roughly mean the Middle Mountains.
The western Sacramento Valley is the homeland of the Patwin, the southern branch of the Wintun peoples.
Their language has two main dialects:
River Patwin, spoken along the Sacramento River, and Hill Patwin, in the hills and plains to the west.
Today Patwin people are citizens of three federally recognized tribes, including the Kletsel Dehe Wintun Nation, headquartered in Williams.
In Williams, Granzella's has served the public since 1976.
The family business includes a restaurant, deli, bakery and sports lounge, and it sells hand-packed jars of olives.
Guy Fieri featured it on the Food Network, including its muffuletta sandwich.
Highway 20 leads about 8 miles east to Colusa, the county seat, on the Sacramento River.
Its name comes from Korusi, a Patwin village that stood on the west bank of the river, where the city is today.
In the 1850 law that created the county, the name was spelled Colusi, and newspapers often wrote Coluse.
Many of the flat fields around here are rice paddies.
In 2024, Colusa County harvested rice from about 118,000 acres, roughly 185 square miles, for a crop of more than half a million tons.
Rice was the county's most valuable crop in 2023, and second only to almonds in 2024.
Sites Reservoir, a lake to come.
In a valley in the hills west of Maxwell, a new lake is planned:
Instead of damming a river, it would be filled with water taken from the Sacramento River during high flows, carried by canals and pumped up into the valley.
Full, it would hold up to 1.5 million acre-feet, enough to serve 7.5 million people for a year.
About 6 miles west of Maxwell stands Swift's Stone Corral, a state historical landmark since 1936.
In 1850, rancher Granville Swift and his partner Frank Sears needed a corral, but there was no timber anywhere around, so they built one out of the flat stones scattered over the land.
About 5 miles east of the freeway lies Delevan National Wildlife Refuge, nearly 5,800 acres of managed marsh and upland.
Each winter more than 200,000 ducks and 100,000 geese come to the refuge.
Visitors can watch wildlife from a simple roadside overlook on the Maxwell-Colusa Highway.
East of here, along the river around Princeton, lay a land grant made out to children.
Thomas Larkin, the United States consul in Monterey, would not become a Mexican citizen, so he could not get land himself.
In 1844 he had three of his children naturalized, and two days later the children received a grant of about 44,000 acres.
The marshes just east of the freeway are the Sacramento National Wildlife Refuge, established in 1937.
On the refuge's own calendar, waterfowl counts average about 1.5 million in October and 1.8 million in November, when geese arrive by the thousands.
The refuge has a visitor center and a 6-mile auto tour.
The mountains on the western skyline are the Coast Range, home of the Mendocino National Forest, which has its headquarters in Willows.
The forest covers about 913,000 acres in six counties, and it is the only national forest in California without a major paved road entering it.
Willows takes its name from a shady watering place ringed by willow trees, where cattle drivers traveling through the valley stopped to rest.
The post office opened in 1862 as Willow, singular, and did not add the s until 1916.
The town has been the seat of Glenn County since the county was created in 1891.
Glenn County is named for Hugh Glenn, a doctor who came west in the Gold Rush and became California's Wheat King.
His land along the Sacramento River grew to 55,000 acres.
At harvest he hired 150 men, and on August 8, 1879, his crews brought in 5,779 bushels of wheat in a single day.
Local belief holds that during World War One, a troop train stopped here for water and the soldiers took offense at the German name.
Petitions to change the post office name succeeded, and on May 21, 1918, Germantown became Artois, after the battles fought in that region of France.
Some of the orchards in the northern Sacramento Valley are prune plums, grown to be dried.
Tehama and Glenn are among California's leading prune counties, and California grows more than 90 percent of the nation's prunes and about 40 percent of the world's.
Harvest runs from mid-August into early September and usually takes about 30 days.
Orland calls itself the Queen Bee Capital of North America.
In 2017 the city council adopted the title because of how many queen bees the town's locally owned commercial apiaries produce.
Orland even has a museum about bees, the Honeybee Discovery Center, and it holds a Queen Bee Festival every June.
East of Orland, on the Sacramento River, lies Hamilton City.

Nearly 4 miles north of town, on December 18, 1883, Will S. Green posted a notice on an oak tree on the river's west bank, claiming 500,000 miner's inches of river water to irrigate the west side of the valley.
The spot is now a state historical landmark.
The freeway crosses Stony Creek just north of Orland.
The creek was named for the loads of rock and sediment it once washed down from the mountains in floods, and it was once called the Capay River.
Today Black Butte Dam, built in 1963 in the foothills to the west, traps most of that sediment.
Rolling Hills Casino, beside the freeway, belongs to the Paskenta Band of Nomlaki Indians, the Hill Nomlaki people of this part of the valley.
In 1959 the federal government terminated the tribe's rancheria and its land was sold.
The Paskenta Band kept its identity and culture and won back full tribal status in 1994.
Many of the orchards in Tehama County are English walnuts.
In 2024 the county had about 31,000 acres of bearing walnut trees, worth about 95 million dollars, its second most valuable crop after almonds.
California grows 99 percent of the commercial walnuts in the United States.
About 8 miles east, near Vina, lay Rancho Bosquejo, the land grant of Peter Lassen, the Danish blacksmith whose name is on Lassen Peak.
In 1848 he led emigrants to his ranch over a new route, the Lassen Cutoff.
Signs his agents later put up promised Gold Rush travelers that the diggings were only 110 miles away, but the cutoff proved about 200 miles longer than the main trails.
Corning began in 1882, when the railroad was extended to this point, and it was named for John Corning, a railroad official.
Its biggest local industry is growing and preparing table olives.
Corning is home to Bell-Carter Foods, maker of Lindsay Olives and the largest table olive processor in the United States.
These rest areas are named for Lieutenant John C. Helmick, the California Highway Patrol's Red Bluff Area commander.
On February 27, 1989, while driving to speak at a Rotary Club luncheon in Oroville, he was killed when his car crashed into a Caltrans truck parked on the shoulder of Highway 99.
The freeway crosses Thomes Creek here, named for Robert Thomes, a pioneer who arrived in the 1840s.
His name has been misspelled so often that official records list the creek as Thomas Creek, Thoms Creek and Toms Creek.
The creek runs about 62 miles from the Coast Range to the Sacramento River, with no permanent dams.
About 5 miles east, on the Sacramento River, is the little city of Tehama, home to 435 people in 2020.
When Tehama County was formed in 1856, Tehama was its county seat, but a county-wide election moved the seat to Red Bluff the very next year.
Because the town floods easily, its houses must sit above flood level, so most have tall stairways to the front door.
East of the freeway, Gerber was platted in 1910 and named for the Gerber family, who owned the town site.
From 1916 to 1965 it was a division point on the Southern Pacific Railroad, where steam locomotives took on fuel, got repairs and changed crews.
The town also had livestock yards and an icing plant for refrigerator cars.
The foothill canyons east of here, along Mill and Deer creeks, are the ancestral homeland of the Yahi, the southernmost group of the Yana people.
After the Gold Rush, settlers killed nearly all of the Yahi; in 1865, about 40 were killed in the Three Knolls Massacre on Mill Creek.
A few survivors hid in the canyons for decades.
The last known Yahi, a man the world came to call Ishi, walked out near Oroville in 1911, starving and alone.
East of the freeway, the Red Bluff Diversion Dam, a concrete structure nearly 6,000 feet long, crosses the Sacramento River.
Finished in 1964, it raised the river to feed the Tehama-Colusa and Corning canals, which water about 150,000 acres of farms.
But it also blocked salmon, so since 2013 its gates have been locked open to let the river run free.
In the fall of 1864, Mary Brown, widow of the abolitionist John Brown, arrived in Red Bluff with her children, poor and homeless.
The town helped her, and a fund headed by Governor Frederick Low raised 450 dollars for a lot and a small house on Main Street.
That house is now a California Historical Landmark.
Red Bluff is named for red bluffs that once stood out along the banks of the Sacramento River, which the freeway crosses twice in town, less than two miles apart.
The town grew up at the head of navigation, the farthest point riverboats could reach, and miners landed here bound for the gold fields of Trinity County.
It was first called Leodocia, then Covertsburg.
A mile north of Red Bluff, on the west bank of the Sacramento River, a state historic park honors William Ide, the only president of the California Republic.
That republic, born in the Bear Flag Revolt, lasted from June 14 to July 9, 1846, less than a month.
research later showed that Ide never owned or lived in the adobe that bears his name.
Red Bluff was home to Alvin Coffey, born enslaved in Kentucky in 1822.
In 1849 his enslaver forced him to California to mine gold, then took him back east and sold him.
Coffey returned to the gold fields, mined enough to buy freedom for himself and his family, and in 1857 the family set out for California and settled in Red Bluff.
East of the freeway lies the little river community of Bend.
It was first called Horsethief Bend, then Sander's Bend, and finally just Bend, after a loop in the Sacramento River nearby.
These rest areas are named for Herbert S. Miles, a highway engineer who spent 42 years working on California's state highways.
As a district engineer, he helped lead the creation of the state's Safety Roadside Rest program.
A plaque honoring him stands at the rest area on the east side of the freeway.
On clear days, the lone peak far off on the northern skyline is Mount Shasta, about 80 miles away.
It rises abruptly, towering nearly 9,800 feet above the land around it.
On a clear winter day, it can be seen from the floor of the Central Valley as far as 140 miles to the south.
The truck scales here are the Cottonwood Commercial Vehicle Enforcement Facility, run by the California Highway Patrol.
Officers and inspectors check trucks and their drivers against North American safety standards and state law.
The first station, on one side of the freeway, opened in 2000, and a second, for trucks going the other way, opened in 2025.
The freeway crosses Cottonwood Creek here, which forms the line between Tehama and Shasta counties along its whole length.
It is the largest undammed tributary of the Sacramento River, which is why it still has runs of Chinook salmon and steelhead.
John C. Frémont named it in 1846, describing cottonwoods along its sandy, gravelly bed.
Cottonwood was a stagecoach town, settled in 1849, and it got its first post office in 1852.
It sits halfway between Redding and Red Bluff, 15 miles from each, on both banks of Cottonwood Creek, which gave it its name.
About 6,300 people live here now, nearly twice as many as in 2010.
About 7 miles east, on Battle Creek, is Coleman National Fish Hatchery, the largest salmon hatchery in the continental United States.
It was built in 1942 to make up for spawning grounds lost when Shasta Dam blocked the river.
Its goal is to raise about 12 million fall-run Chinook salmon each year.
On clear days, the big mountain on the eastern skyline is Lassen Peak, about 40 miles away, the southernmost active volcano in the Cascade Range.
On May 22, 1915, it blasted a column of ash more than 30,000 feet into the sky.
A photograph of that eruption was taken from Red Bluff, about 45 miles from the peak.
In 1872, a rancher and hotel keeper named Elias Anderson deeded the Central Pacific Railroad a right of way through his land, and in return the railroad named its depot after him.
Today Anderson is a city of about 11,000, and it is the headquarters of Sierra Pacific Industries.
Clear Creek joins the Sacramento River just west of the freeway, south of Redding.
Five miles up the creek, at a spot called Reading's Bar, Pierson B. Reading and his Native workers found gold in 1848.
Both the creek and Reading's Bar are now state historical landmarks.
West of the freeway, south of Redding, is the Redding Rancheria, a federally recognized tribe of Wintu, Pit River and Yana people.
Its 31-acre site was bought by the Bureau of Indian Affairs in 1922, as a place to camp and live for Native people who had been made landless by settlers.
On April 5, 1846, an armed expedition led by Captain John C. Frémont attacked a large Wintu camp on the banks of the Sacramento River near what is now Redding.
The Wintu, most of them women and children, were trapped against the river.
Estimates of the dead range from 125 to 900, and no one was ever punished.
On July 26, 2018, the Carr Fire jumped the Sacramento River into the west side of Redding, and 38,000 people had to evacuate.
That evening a fire whirl formed, with winds estimated above 143 miles an hour, as strong as an EF3 tornado, and it rose an estimated 18,000 feet into the sky.
During the Gold Rush, miners found little gold in this ground, and the spot was called Poverty Flats.
In 1868 the Central Pacific Railroad's land agent, Benjamin Redding, bought land here for a northern terminus, and the railroad built a town and named it for him.
West of the freeway, the Sundial Bridge, a 700-foot footbridge designed by Santiago Calatrava, crosses the Sacramento River.
Its 217-foot mast points due north at a 42-degree angle and casts its shadow on a giant dial.
The tip of that shadow moves about a foot a minute, so you can watch the Earth turn.
Highway 299 leads to Shasta, about six miles west of Redding.
In the 1850s it was the largest town in the area and the county seat, home to some 3,500 people.
Then in 1873 the railroad bypassed it for Redding, and Shasta faded into a near ghost town.
Its row of Gold Rush brick buildings is now a state historic park.
To make concrete for Shasta Dam, builders needed mountains of sand and gravel.
So they built what was then the largest conveyor belt system in the world, 9.5 miles long, running from Redding to the dam site.
It could carry 1,100 tons of material an hour.
The city of Shasta Lake grew out of five small communities that sprang up in 1938, when work began on Shasta Dam:
Central Valley, Project City, Summit City, Pine Grove and Toyon.
Pine Grove stood where Pine Grove Avenue now meets the freeway.
The communities did not join into one city until 1993.
Shasta Dam stands about four miles west, 602 feet tall.
When it was finished in 1945, 26 months earlier than planned, only Hoover Dam was taller.
During World War II, with so many men gone to fight, many of the workers were women and high school students.
One workman reportedly summed it up:
Old Shasta's about the secondest dam there is.
Under Shasta Lake lies Kennett, once the largest mining town in the area outside Redding and Shasta.
Its two biggest mines held unusually pure copper ore.
There's no record of any public hearing to ask residents before it was flooded.
By 1944 the whole town was underwater, and it now sits under roughly 400 feet of water, depending on the lake level.
Before the lake, old Highway 99 ran through Mountain Gate and then plunged into the valley that Shasta Lake now fills.
In drought years, when the water falls, old bridges, road cuts and guardrails come back into view.
Near the Bridge Bay exit stands a marker to the stagecoach days.
The California and Oregon stage road crossed the top of Bass Hill here and dropped down to the Pit River, and the hill was a favorite spot for bandit holdups.
The marker honors the stage drivers under the title Pioneers Who Held the Ribbons.
Shasta Lake is California's largest reservoir, with 365 miles of steep, wooded shoreline.
It has four big arms, made by the Sacramento River, the McCloud River, the Pit River and Sulanharas Creek.
The Pit River Bridge is a double-decker.
I-5 rides the top deck and the railroad runs underneath.
Built in 1942, it stands about 500 feet above the old bed of the Pit River, making it the highest double-deck bridge in the United States.
When the lake is full, though, the water comes within about 40 feet of the bridge.
Just north of the Pit River Bridge, the two directions of I-5 split apart, leaving what is said to be the second-largest median in California.
Only Interstate 8's In-Ko-Pah grade has a bigger one.
The limestone hills around this lake hide salamanders found nowhere else on Earth.
Scientists once thought there was just one kind.
In 2018 they found three, including the Wintu Shasta salamander, which lives on the lake's north shore near the McCloud River.
Getting to these limestone caves takes a catamaran ride across the lake's McCloud arm and then a bus ride up a steep mountain road.
The caves sit about 900 feet above the lake.
Inside, the words James Richardson wrote on the wall on November 11, 1878, claiming the discovery, are still clearly legible.
The McCloud River arm of this lake is the homeland of the Winnemem Wintu, whose name means middle water people or middle river people.
When the lake filled, scores of their village sites, burial grounds and sacred places went underwater.
They have long sought federal recognition, and they oppose plans to raise the dam.
On June 30, 2021, a fire started beside I-5 near the Salt Creek exit and shut down the freeway.
Forest officials believe it was likely sparked by hot material that fell from a vehicle on the interstate.
It destroyed 27 homes and 14 other buildings around Lakehead.
In 1872, the nation's first federal fish hatchery opened on the McCloud River, which now flows into this lake.
Livingston Stone built it at a spot where he found Wintu people catching Chinook salmon.
Its eggs were shipped across the country and as far as Japan and New Zealand.
Lakehead sits on the northern shore of Shasta Lake.
About 470 people lived here in 2020, and in summer more than 1,500 seasonal residents can join them.
In 1992, Caltrans finished upgrading a final 13-mile stretch of I-5 north of Lakehead.
When the railroad pushed up this canyon in the 1880s, the town of Delta was the end of the line for about two years.
Lots sold for 45 to 185 dollars, and almost overnight there were saloons, hotels, a Wells Fargo office and a turntable for the engines.
The 39-mile train ride to Redding took two hours and 20 minutes.
The river beside the freeway is the upper Sacramento.

It begins near Mount Shasta, where its North, Middle and South forks meet, passes through Lake Siskiyou, and then runs about 60 miles through this canyon, past Dunsmuir and Castella, to Shasta Lake near Lakehead.
Up here it is a blue ribbon trout stream, where wild rainbow trout abound.
Near the Pollard Flat exit was Portuguese Flat, a Gold Rush camp of the early 1850s made up largely of Portuguese miners.
It had rich diggings and a reputation as one of the roughest camps in northern Shasta County.
By 1885 it seems to have been deserted, and its site lies along what is now I-5.
The river, the railroad and the freeway all squeeze through this one canyon.
The railroad follows the old Siskiyou Trail.
Amtrak's Coast Starlight still runs these tracks every day on its trips between Los Angeles and Seattle.
The name of this exit goes back to Simeon Southern, nicknamed Sims, who opened a log stage station and hotel here in 1859, where travelers stopped to rest and eat for 50 years.
The settlement of Hazel Creek took the name Sims in 1871, since his station was the center of town.
In September 1880, President Rutherford B. Hayes stayed here with Generals Sherman and Sheridan.
Long before this was a freeway, it was a web of Native American footpaths between California and the Northwest.
In the 1820s, Hudson's Bay Company fur trappers followed them south from the Columbia River, and the route became known as the Siskiyou Trail.
I-5 follows the same path today.
The country around Castle Crags is the ancestral home of the Okwanuchu Shasta people.
The Crags have long been revered by the Wintu, Achumawi and Modoc peoples too, and the area's streams, river and springs are considered sacred.
The Gold Rush brought thousands of miners and terrible violence, and in June 1855 miners fought Modoc people below Battle Rock, now marked at the state park entrance.
In the 1890s, mineral water from a spring here was bottled and shipped all over the world.
The bottling company went broke in the 1929 crash, and in 1943 the state bought 925 acres of the old springs property.
That was the start of Castle Crags State Park, which has 28 miles of trails and a vista point facing the Crags and Mount Shasta.
These granite spires rise from about 2,000 feet at the river to more than 6,500 feet at the top.
The granite formed underground in the Jurassic period, the age of dinosaurs, and Ice Age glaciers later scraped away the softer rock around it.
A bellflower that grows here is found nowhere else in the world.
Just off this exit, a lodge founded in 1968 lets guests sleep in old cabooses and eat in a restaurant inside an original train car, with Castle Crags towering above.
Once called Railroad Park Resort, it now goes by Jubilee Railroad.
Dunsmuir was a railroad town first, nicknamed Pusher, because extra steam engines were added here to push trains up the steep grades north of town.
In 1888, Alexander Dunsmuir, son of a British Columbia coal baron, offered the town a fountain if it would take his name.
Its slogan calls it the Home of the Best Water on Earth, filtered through Mount Shasta's lava.
Under the freeway in north Dunsmuir lies Upper Soda Springs, now a riverside park.
Okwanuchu people camped here during salmon season, at a wide, shallow spot they called the place to cross the river.
In the early 1850s it became home to the area's first non-Native settlers, and later to a toll bridge, a stage hotel and a springhouse serving soda water from the mineral springs.
In 1924, New York Yankees stars Babe Ruth and Bob Meusel came to Dunsmuir on a barnstorming tour and played an exhibition game against the locals in the city park.
That park is now home to a botanical garden along the river.
A short trail from this exit leads to a waterfall with a small cave behind it, so you can walk behind the falling water.
There's also a viewing platform over the river with a view of Mount Shasta.
Being so close to I-5, it's a popular stop for passing drivers.
Just north of Dunsmuir was Shasta Springs, a summer resort on the railroad main line in the late 1800s and early 1900s.
Natural springs here were the original source of the water and drinks that became the Shasta brand of soft drinks.
On the night of July 14, 1991, a train derailed at a horseshoe curve called the Cantara Loop, upstream from Dunsmuir, and a tank car spilled about 19,000 gallons of pesticide into the river.
More than a million fish died.
It's still the largest hazardous chemical spill in California history, but the river has largely recovered.
Highway 89 heads east to McCloud, a lumber company town on the southern slope of Mount Shasta.
For decades the company mill supplied the homes with electricity and even steam heat.
The houses passed to private owners in 1965, and the mill closed for good in 2002.
On Old Stage Road in Mount Shasta, the Mount Shasta Hatchery has raised trout since 1888, and the state calls it the oldest trout hatchery west of the Mississippi.
It supplies most of the eggs for the state's trout hatcheries, upwards of 30 million a year.
From mid-March through July, visitors can watch the eggs hatch and the baby fish grow.
This town was called Strawberry Valley, then Berryvale, then Sisson, after Justin Sisson, who gave the land for the railroad station.
It officially became the City of Mount Shasta in 1925.
It sits at about 3,600 feet, less than 9 miles from the summit, and gets nearly 103 inches of snow in a typical winter.
In Mount Shasta City Park, water pours straight out of a hillside at Big Springs.
It started as glacial melt and spent more than 50 years filtering through volcanic rock.
About 12 million gallons a day flow out here and help start the Sacramento River.
By volume, about 85 cubic miles, it is the biggest stratovolcano in the Cascade Range, and seven glaciers ring its slopes.
Its last major eruption was about 3,000 years ago, and the U.S. Geological Survey rates it a very high threat volcano.
Mount Shasta has a famous legend:
a hidden city on the mountain, home to advanced beings from a lost continent called Lemuria.
The story grew from a passing mention in the 1880s into a whole book in 1931.
No one has ever found the city.
The dark cone close beside the freeway is Black Butte, a cluster of lava domes that squeezed out about 9,000 to 10,000 years ago.
I-5 crosses a 3,912-foot pass at its western base, called Black Butte Summit.
The smaller peak on Mount Shasta's west side is Shastina, about 12,330 feet tall.
That's taller than Mount Adams in Washington.
The big gash down its side facing Weed is Diller Canyon, cut by hot volcanic flows, and it drops more than 7,000 vertical feet.
The big peak west of the freeway is Mount Eddy, 9,037 feet tall, the highest point in the Trinity Mountains.
It's made mostly of a rock called serpentinized peridotite.
Mount Eddy is the highest summit west of I-5 anywhere in the United States.
About 12 miles northeast of Weed is Pluto's Cave, a lava tube roughly 190,000 years old.
A man named Nelson Cash stumbled onto it in 1863 while looking for stray cattle, and it was named for Pluto, the god of the underworld.
Visitors can hike about 1,200 feet inside.
Weed is named for Abner Weed, who found that the strong winds here were good for drying lumber.
In 1897 he bought a mill and 280 acres for 400 dollars.
The town motto is Weed like to welcome you, and over the years its road signs have had a habit of disappearing.
On September 15, 2014, the wind-driven Boles Fire spread through Weed and destroyed more than 150 buildings, most of them homes, in a single day.
On September 2, 2022, the Mill Fire started at the lumber mill north of town and burned the Lincoln Heights neighborhood.
This exit is the end of State Route 265, North Weed Boulevard.
It's only two blocks long, which makes it the second-shortest state highway in California.
Gray wolves have returned to Siskiyou County.
In late December 2011, a collared wolf from Oregon known as OR-7 crossed the state line, the first wild wolf confirmed in California since 1924.
In 2015 a trail camera in Siskiyou County confirmed the Shasta Pack, two adults and five pups, the state's first resident wolf pack in more than a century.
A two-lane county road called Old Highway 99 runs between Weed and Yreka, still in the same form it had when it was U.S. 99, the main West Coast highway before I-5.
It roughly parallels the freeway, but at one point swings several miles away.
West of the freeway sits Gazelle, a tiny town of about 95 people.
Its post office took the name Gazelle in 1870.
A gazelle is a small African antelope, and in the 1850s a steamer called the Gazelle also ran between San Francisco and the upper Sacramento River.
See the little lumpy hills scattered across the flat valley?
Hundreds of thousands of years ago, an older version of Mount Shasta collapsed in one of the largest landslides known on Earth.
The debris spread across more than 170 square miles of Shasta Valley, and these hummocks are the pieces.
Shasta Valley is one of Siskiyou County's four main farming areas.
Alfalfa hay is the county's biggest field crop:
in 2023, farmers cut about 175,000 tons of it from some 29,000 acres.
Ranchers counted around 45,000 cattle and calves at the start of that year.
Siskiyou County's most valuable farm product isn't hay or cattle.
In 2023 the county grew them on more than 2,800 acres, at about 360,000 plants per acre.
That adds up to roughly a billion young plants, worth about 184 million dollars.
About five miles east, near Montague, the state's Shasta Valley Wildlife Area protects some 4,700 acres of juniper woodland, riverside forest, wetlands and fields, with Mount Shasta as its backdrop.
Sandhill cranes, waterfowl, birds of prey and shorebirds all use it.
On November 27, 1941, young men waving hunting rifles stopped traffic on U.S. 99 south of Yreka and handed out a proclamation of independence for the State of Jefferson.
They promised to secede every Thursday until further notice.
The movement's seal is a gold pan with two Xs, called the Double Cross, for feeling abandoned by both state capitals.
In March 1851, a mule packer named Abraham Thompson found gold here, and by April, 2,000 miners had arrived at what they called Thompson's Dry Diggings.
The name Yreka comes from waik'a, the Shasta people's word for Mount Shasta.
Mark Twain told a funnier story:
a bakery sign seen backwards, BAKERY without the B, read YREKA.
When the Southern Pacific laid its main line through Shasta Valley in the 1880s, it skipped Yreka for a shorter, more level route through Montague.
So the people of Yreka built their own railroad.
The Yreka Railroad opened in January 1889 and connected the town to the main line at Montague.
The Shasta River starts on Mount Eddy and runs 58 miles through Shasta Valley to the Klamath.
North of Yreka, the freeway crosses it, and the river then slips into a canyon.
It's a spawning river for Chinook salmon, and estimates say about 80,000 adult fish once returned to it every year.
Shasta Valley and the nearby Klamath River are part of the homeland of the Shasta people, and the people of the Shasta River were known as the Ahotireitsu.
Women and children dove in the Klamath for mussels.
Today Shasta people live in Yreka and on the Quartz Valley Indian Reservation, and on the Grand Ronde and Siletz reservations in Oregon.
The rugged, forested mountains to the west are the Klamath Mountains.
Their rocks began as volcanic islands and pieces of other continents out in the Pacific, some as old as 500 million years, that later crashed into North America.
They hold one of the richest mixes of cone-bearing trees on Earth, about 30 kinds.
This rest area by the Klamath River honors State Senator Randolph Collier, who lived in Siskiyou County nearly all his life.
He co-wrote the 1947 law that laid the groundwork for California's freeway system, so in a way, you're driving on his idea.
The freeway crosses the Klamath River near here, where the river turns sharply south to meet I-5.
Upstream, four hydroelectric dams were torn down in 2023 and 2024, the largest dam removal in American history.
On October 17, 2024, a fall-run Chinook salmon was spotted in Oregon's Upper Klamath Basin, the first to reach it in more than 100 years.
Highway 96 follows the Klamath River west into Karuk country.
Karuk means upriver, and traditionally the Karuk called themselves the middle of the world people.
The Karuk Tribe is one of the largest tribes in California, and the 2010 census counted about 6,100 Karuk people.
Nobody is sure where the name Siskiyou comes from.
One story says it was a Cree word for a bob-tailed horse.
Another says Hudson's Bay Company trappers gave a river ford the French name Six Cailloux, six stones, and that the name was later borrowed for a crossing on the Klamath River near Hornbrook.

Traffic entering California on I-5 stops here, near Hornbrook, at one of 16 agricultural inspection stations that the California Department of Food and Agriculture runs where major highways cross into the state.
Inspectors look for pests in plants or cargo that could harm California's farms.
Passenger cars with California or neighboring-state plates usually get just a few questions about what they carry.
Hilt has the northernmost I-5 exit in California.
It grew up as a company town, first for the Northern California Lumber Company and then for the Fruit Growers Supply Company, an affiliate of Sunkist.
It's named for an early settler, John Hilt.
The California and Oregon border follows the 42nd parallel, a line set in an 1819 treaty between the United States and Spain.
When California became a state in 1850, it kept that line as its northern border.
A survey around 1870 marked it with errors, creating a dispute that continues to this day.

The main port was built in 1973, and a $741 million rebuild that took nearly ten years was finished in 2019.
Trucks have crossed at the Otay Mesa port since 1983.
The lanes into Mexico now pass through a Mexican gateway called El Chaparral, which roughly tripled them to 22.
Waits to enter the United States can still stretch to several hours.

Kumeyaay tradition holds that the people have lived around San Diego since 10,000 BC.
The Spanish called them Diegueños, after Mission San Diego, and in Mexico they are known as Kumiai.
Before Cabrillo landed in 1542, trail runners carrying messages between bands had already spread word of the strangers.
Families and ceremonies still cross the line, and about 1,900 Kumiai came to hold special visas to attend events on the US side.
Bird songs, which recount migrations and ancestral history, are still sung at gatherings.
In 2020, as border wall construction sped up, Kumeyaay women led protests, and the La Posta Band sued to stop building through a sacred burial ground.

The river runs only after rains, and it floods.
Floods in 1891 and 1895 washed out Tia Juana City, an 1887 settlement where the outlet mall by the border stands now.
In 1908, William Smythe started the Little Landers colony nearby, where each member farmed about 2 acres and all the buying and selling was shared.
The colony took the name San Ysidro, an old spelling of Saint Isidore the Laborer, and lasted until a great flood wiped out its farms in 1916.
Today a regional park of more than 1,800 acres fills much of the valley, with trails for walking and horseback riding, and big winter waves off the river mouth have drawn surfers since at least 1937.
In 2020, a trade agreement set aside $300 million to fight the river's pollution.

Montgomery shaped his first glider's wing on the curve of a seagull's.
He steered it up and down with a movable elevator and tipped it side to side by shifting his weight.
The glider handled side gusts poorly, so he studied turkey vultures and gave his next glider hinged wing flaps, an early form of the ailerons on airplanes today.
The Montgomerys' 1880s Fruitland Ranch stood where this freeway now runs, and in 1949 the road from the border to downtown San Diego was named the John J. Montgomery Freeway.
He later taught at Santa Clara College and died in a glider crash in San Jose in 1911.

Hatfield called himself a moisture accelerator.
He brewed a secret mix of 23 chemicals in evaporating tanks, and for San Diego he built a tower beside Lake Morena.
The storms overflowed the Sweetwater Dam too, washed away bridges, stranded trains and cut phone lines.
Afterward the council refused to pay unless Hatfield accepted the blame for damages, with claims already at $3.5 million.
He sued, and in 1938 the courts ruled the rain an act of God, so he was cleared but never paid.
A San Diego mayor who studied his record called him nothing more than a darned good weather prophet.

On the West Coast, only San Francisco Bay and San Diego Bay have the natural conditions for making sea salt.
The very salty ponds breed brine shrimp and brine flies, a feast for birds, and they sit inside the San Diego Bay National Wildlife Refuge.
Ninety-four kinds of birds use the area, and a 2010 count found more than 20,000 birds, including endangered California least terns.
The 1916 flood wiped out the ponds, and rebuilding took until the 1950s.
As late as 1978 the works supplied the salt for San Diego's tuna fleet.
When its little narrow-gauge salt railway was torn out in the 1970s, the spot where it crossed over a full-size railroad was kept, the only such crossing in the United States.

Lemons were introduced by a retired professor from the University of Wisconsin.
By 1911 growers earned about $2,000 an acre, and lemon sales topped $400,000 a year.
Japanese American farmers made celery a big crop too, and in 1931 lemons brought in $1 million and celery $600,000.
Then, in 1941, Rohr Aircraft moved to town, and its 11,000 workers built power units for B-24 Liberator bombers.
With workers off at war or at the factory, the farmland was sold, and the groves never came back.
The city's Lemon Festival still pays tribute to them.

The Kumeyaay fished, hunted and gathered here.

From 1916 to 1920, the Hercules Powder Company ran a 30-acre plant on this shore, turning kelp into acetone and potash, a key ingredient in smokeless gunpowder during World War I. The site is now known as Gunpowder Point.

The refuge also holds the Living Coast Discovery Center, a zoo and aquarium that opened in 1987 as the Chula Vista Nature Interpretive Center, with green sea turtles, sharks, rays and bald and golden eagles.
Trails lead 1.5 miles out to the bay, and more than 200 kinds of birds have been recorded on the refuge.

Frank Kimball's house had a bathtub and hot running water, and it was called the first modern house in the county.
The brothers built the area's first roads and railroad, a post office and a wharf.
In 1882 the California Southern Railroad built a depot here, the first Pacific Coast terminal of the Santa Fe Railway.
When transcontinental trains arrived in November 1885, one of the biggest land booms in California history began.
The Italianate depot is the only survivor of the five original transcontinental terminal stations.
Later, sailors' bars earned National Avenue the nickname Mile of Bars, and the city remade it as the Mile of Cars, one of the first auto malls in the world.

In 1918, a company building concrete ships for World War I used this shore.
When that business faded, the Navy took over, and in February 1922 the site opened as the Destroyer Base, San Diego.
In 1924 alone, it took 77 destroyers out of service.
During World War II it was renamed the Repair Base, and from 1943 to 1945 its crews repaired, overhauled or converted more than 5,000 ships.
It became the Pacific Fleet's main home port after the Long Beach Naval Shipyard closed in 1994.
National City's three-mile bayfront is part of the base.

Barrio Logan, a mostly Mexican American neighborhood, was split in two when this freeway came through in 1963, and the bridge ramps divided it again in 1969.
More than 5,000 homes and businesses were removed.
The city promised a park, but on April 22, 1970, a student named Mario Solis found bulldozers preparing a Highway Patrol parking lot instead.
Neighbors and students occupied the land for twelve days, planting trees, flowers and cactus, until the city agreed to build the park.
Artist Salvador Torres proposed turning the gray concrete pillars into a giant canvas, and painting began in 1973.
The park became a National Historic Landmark in 2016, and every April the neighborhood celebrates Chicano Park Day.

The first shop, at India and Grape streets, made tortillas by hand.
In 1947 the family moved to 3695 India Street and began selling taquitos and other Sonoran-style dishes.
Los Angeles has a rival claim to the taquito's early days:
Cielito Lindo, opened on Olvera Street in 1934.
The Pesqueira family still runs El Indio.

In 1927 the Ryan company built the Spirit of St. Louis near here for Charles Lindbergh's flight across the Atlantic.
Proud of that, San Diego voted bonds in 1928 for an airport, and Lindbergh lent it his name.
It was dedicated that August as Lindbergh Field, while 140 Navy and 82 Army planes flew over.
During World War II, Consolidated Aircraft built warplanes next door, and a street here is still named Liberator Way, after its B-24 Liberator.
The name changed to San Diego International Airport in 2003.
Most landings come in from the east, over downtown, because the usual winds blow from the west, and a curfew fines takeoffs between 11:30 at night and 6:30 in the morning.

When the Portolá expedition arrived in 1769, the crews of its supply ships were dying of scurvy and thirst, and the people of Kosa'aay, whose name means drying out place, gave them food and water.
The Spanish then set up a hospital camp on the hill and took over the village's water source, and less than a month after the mission was founded, the Kumeyaay fought back.
In 1774 the mission moved a few miles up the valley, where Mission San Diego de Alcalá still stands.
Old Town was the heart of San Diego until the 1860s, when Alonzo Horton's New Town by the harbor, today's downtown, drew people away.
The Spanish Revival Serra Museum on the hilltop was given to the city by George Marston in 1929, and nothing of the old fort survives above ground.

From the exit, follow Interstate 8 east to the Mission Gorge Road exit, then Twain Avenue.
The mission began on a hill near the harbor and moved here in 1774.

Before 1821 it usually emptied into San Diego Bay, until a flood that fall swung it into False Bay in a single night, though no rain fell on the coast.

The name Mission Bay comes from an 1888 poem by Rose Hartwick Thorpe.
Dredging left only about 5 percent of the old wetlands.

The trees here are protected in Torrey Pines State Natural Reserve, 2,000 acres of cliffs and trails.
It began in 1899, when George Marston persuaded the city to set aside 364 acres, and newspaperwoman Ellen Browning Scripps later bought more land and gave it to the city.

Crosby helped write the song Where the Turf Meets the Surf that year to promote the track.

From their tops the rocks look out over much of the San Joaquin Valley, including the approaches to Arroyo de Cantua, where the gang kept its rancho.

He noticed the three rocks on the skyline and named the little town he founded there Three Rocks.

As proof, the rangers cut off the head they said was Murrieta's and the hand of his associate Three-Fingered Jack, and kept them in a jar of alcohol to collect their reward.
The jar toured California, and people paid a dollar to look.
That August, a letter to a San Francisco newspaper claimed the rangers had killed innocent mustang catchers.
Evidence for a real Murrieta is thin, but the legend grew, helped along by an 1854 novel by John Rollin Ridge, a Cherokee writer.
The head was destroyed in the 1906 San Francisco earthquake and fire.

Mendota Dam, built in 1871 where the river meets Fresno Slough, first sent water into the Main Canal for riverside farmland.
Since 1951 the Delta-Mendota Canal has ended at the pool behind it, bringing Delta water through 117 miles of canal from near Tracy.
Fresno Slough can flow either way:
north into the river in the rainy season, and south toward the Tulare Lake basin in the dry months.
In the years after the Gold Rush, a nearby settlement called Las Juntas was a haven for fugitives, visited by the bandits Joaquin Murrieta and Tiburcio Vasquez.

California's pistachio orchards grew from about 106,000 acres in 2002 to 554,000 acres in 2022, because the hardy trees can thrive with the somewhat salty water and soil found in parts of the Central Valley.
Fresno County alone grew about 40 percent of the country's pistachios in 2021, and in 2017 it ranked second in the state for cotton.
In 2000 the county used more fresh water each day than any other county in the United States, about 3.7 billion gallons.
Here's a story while we drive, about The nation's top farm county.
Farmers say federal rules meant to protect smelt and salmon have cut their water.
In June 2011 the Associated Press reported several hundred new signs along I-5 and Highway 99, with lines like Man-made drought and Food grows where water flows.
Farmers with the newest federal water contracts are the first to face cuts, the report noted, which is why West Side farmers got the least water during that drought.
It also cited a Congressional Research Service report finding that less than a quarter of the cuts in supply came from endangered species protections, and that most came from the drought itself.
Environmentalists said the signs gave a false picture of the drought and its causes.
The group was founded in 2000 by Denis Prosperi, a Madera almond and wine grape farmer, and in 2015 it ran solely on donations.

The valley was in its sixth year of drought, the rainy season had not begun, and fields near the road had been plowed and left bare, with no crops to hold the dust.
The nearest weather station tracking wind, at Naval Air Station Lemoore, recorded gusts of 48 miles an hour.
Most of the crashes happened in five groups along a mile and a half of freeway, and several vehicles caught fire.
A fire truck and an ambulance crashed on the way in, yet rescuers reached the site within half an hour.
About 150 miles of I-5 were closed for a day.

Other coastal ranges to the west catch most of the ocean's rain, so these mountains stay dry, mostly rolling grassland, chaparral and oak woodland, and most of the land is private ranches.
The range is part of the homelands of many Native peoples, including the Ohlone, Yokuts, Miwok, Amah Mutsun and Salinan.
It also shelters a millipede found only in the southern part of the range, Illacme plenipes, which can have as many as 750 legs.
Until 2021, no animal known to science had more.
It was first found in 1926 and not seen again until 2005.

From Los Angeles the road crossed Tejon Pass and came down through the San Emigdio Mountains into the valley.
Its Spanish names for creeks and watering places described what travelers found:
Arroyo de las Garzas, Creek of the Herons, and Aguaje de las Berendas, Waterhole of the Pronghorns, in Merced County, and Arroyo de las Polvarduras, Creek of the Dust Storms, in Fresno County.
The road was favored by those who wanted to stay out of sight of Spanish officials on the coast.
Later, Californio vaqueros drove cattle along it, while mustang catchers herded wild horses to the Bay Area, Southern California and Sonora.
At its north end the road turned west over the Diablo Range at Corral Hollow Pass.
Through Santa Nella, its route has been replaced by Interstate 5 and Highway 33.

Poland spent 50 years studying sinking land and became known as Mr. Land Subsidence.
When too much groundwater is pumped out, loose layers underground compact, and past a certain point the ground cannot spring back.
The sinking began in the 1920s, and by 1970 more than a foot of it had spread across about 5,200 square miles, about half the valley.
It was first discovered in the 1950s, and a network to measure it was built in the 1960s.
The sinking has cut how much water the Delta-Mendota Canal can carry and has meant expensive repairs to canals, including the California Aqueduct.

West of the hills lies Panoche Valley, home to endangered animals such as the San Joaquin kit fox, the giant kangaroo rat and the blunt-nosed leopard lizard.
Its grasslands are critical habitat, especially in winter, for birds such as golden eagles, ferruginous hawks, prairie falcons, mountain plovers and long-billed curlews.
The hills themselves hold fossils of ancient cold seeps from the Mesozoic era, the age of dinosaurs.
The Bureau of Land Management keeps motor vehicles out of its Panoche Hills recreation area from mid-April to mid-October, the fire season.

Far upstream, in the southern Diablo Range near its highest peak, are the old New Idria mines, which dug mercury from 1854 until 1972 and were at one time the second most productive mercury mines in the country.
Gold Rush miners needed mercury to pull gold out of ore, and before New Idria and New Almaden it came almost entirely from Europe.
The mines left behind a ghost town with more than 100 standing buildings, and mercury from the old workings has polluted the creeks that feed Panoche Creek.
In 2011 the site was listed for federal Superfund cleanup.

Native people knew the springs long before settlers came, and they showed them to a sheepherder named John Merci, who later spelled his name Mercy.

During the Gold Rush the spot was a watering place called Aguaje Panochita, where mustang catchers held captured horses, and it was a stop for the gang known as the Five Joaquins as they drove horses south to their hideout on Cantua Creek.
In 1912 San Francisco developer Frederick Bourn bought the springs and built cabins and a hotel.
The hotel burned in the mid-1930s and was replaced by a bathhouse and restaurant.
Little Panoche Road itself was once part of a stagecoach route.
Here's a story while we drive, about Mercey Hot Springs.
Little Panoche Creek, which comes out of the hills near here, shows how much the canals have changed the land.
Before irrigation, its water may have reached a slough of the San Joaquin River in very wet years.
Today it flows through Little Panoche Reservoir and simply ends in the aqueduct.
Its old Spanish name, Arroyita de Panoche, meant Little Sugarloaf Creek, and it was a watering place on El Camino Viejo.
Here's a story while we drive, about The San Luis Canal.
In 1857 Firebaugh built a wagon road with a gentler grade over Pacheco Pass, replacing a steep, rough horse and mule trail that ran near today's Highway 152.
In the 1880s the land around his ferry was part of the huge holdings of Miller and Lux, whose cattle operation covered the country from Dos Palos to Mendota.
It holds a yearly Cantaloupe Round-Up to celebrate the melon harvest, which peaks in late July.

A small treatment system cleans gray water so it can be used again to flush the toilets, which cuts the rest area's need for water from the state system during droughts.
The landscaping uses native, drought-tolerant plants, the plaza's design was inspired by aerial views of farmland, and graphics honor the region's Basque history.
The parking areas took more than 180,000 cubic feet of concrete, 9 inches thick for cars and 12 inches thick for trucks.
That light-colored concrete reflects sunlight, which helps keep the air cooler.

Before irrigation, the San Joaquin and its branches had the third largest salmon run in California, likely 200,000 to 500,000 spawning fish a year.
With most of its water now held behind Friant Dam and sent into canals, long stretches often run dry.

In 2009 the federal government began releasing water from Friant again to restore two dry stretches, about 64 miles in all, part of one of the largest river recovery efforts in the country, with salmon to be brought back.
irrigators lost some water, and a lawsuit claimed the new flows were seeping through old levees onto farmland near Los Banos.

The plant was built between 1963 and 1966 as part of the State Water Project.
Its name means two friends in Spanish.
Its water arrives through about 16 miles of canal from O'Neill Forebay.
A vista point called Dos Amigos sits beside the freeway nearby.

Each autumn more than 20,000 cranes and 60,000 Arctic-nesting geese fly in from Alaska and Canada to spend about six months at Merced National Wildlife Refuge, part of the Grasslands.
It holds the largest wintering flocks of lesser sandhill cranes and Ross's geese on the Pacific Flyway.
The refuge was set up in 1951 to draw wintering ducks and geese away from nearby farm fields, where they were damaging crops.
In spring, wildflowers bloom in rings around drying vernal pools, the kind of color that led John Muir to call the valley floor the floweriest part of the world he had seen.

The town moved to its present site in 1889, when the railroad arrived.
Cattle baron Henry Miller ran his valley empire from Canal Farm here, set up in 1873, and in the late 1800s he was one of the largest landowners in the United States.
Uriah Wood, the area's first Anglo-American settler, once raced Miller to the land office in Stockton to file a claim.
After crossing the San Joaquin River, Wood paid the ferryman five dollars to hold the boat on the east side, and won his land for 45 cents an acre.
A 10-acre plaza downtown honors Miller with a big bronze of him and his cattle.

Chris Rufer started Morning Star in 1970 as an owner-operator trucker, hauling tomatoes from fields to canneries.
The company is known for having no bosses:
workers define their own job duties, and pay is based on reviews from coworkers.
Its factories can handle more than 3,000 tons of tomatoes an hour, and at harvest time more than 2,500 seasonal workers join about 550 year-round employees.
As of 2023 it supplied about a tenth of the world's ingredient tomato products.

The refuge has played a vital role in the recovery of tule elk, which were nearly wiped out in the 1800s.
In March 1978, ten tule elk from Merced County, two males and eight females, were moved to Tomales Point at Point Reyes, where the herd struggled at first, then began growing fast in 1981.
The refuge visitor center has an exhibit hall with displays and a place to view tule elk.
From there, a Tule Elk auto tour route and a Waterfowl route wind through the refuge, and in hot months the elk are easiest to see in the morning or early evening.

The pass is named for Francisco Perez Pacheco, a Californio rancher.
In the 1850s travelers called it Robber's Pass because of frequent holdups.
Pacheco Pass Station was a stop on the Butterfield Overland Mail stagecoach route, which linked St. Louis with San Francisco from 1858 to 1861.
California's high-speed rail line is planned to run beneath the pass in the Pacheco Pass Tunnels, about 13 miles long, which are expected to be the longest rail tunnels in North America.

On August 18, 1962, President John F. Kennedy and Governor Pat Brown gave the signal for the first blasts at the dam site, in front of 15,000 people.
The valley it flooded is Yokuts homeland, later part of Rancho San Luis Gonzaga, and the reservoir first filled on May 31, 1969.
Between the dam and O'Neill Forebay, the Gianelli Pumping-Generating Plant works like a giant water battery.

When demand for electricity is low, its eight reversible units pump water up into the reservoir, and when demand is high, the water runs back down through the same machines, which can make 424 megawatts.
Only about 70 percent of the pumping energy comes back, but selling power at peak times helps pay for the State Water Project's giant pumps.
A plan approved in 2023 would raise the dam 10 feet by 2032.

The ranch failed after many of its horses escaped into the valley, followed by fighting with Native people.
The spot stayed a stopping place:
it sat on El Camino Viejo, and in the Gold Rush the stage road from Hill's Ferry crossed San Luis Creek here on its way to Pacheco Pass.
Basque sheepmen built a two-story adobe nearby in the 1860s, and Miller and Lux later replaced it with a frame house that stood until the 1960s, when a roadside stop took its place.
Santa Nella is still mostly a place for travelers to stop.

Danish-born Anton Andersen and his French-born wife, Juliette, opened their first cafe in 1924 and named it for their proudest possession, a new electric stove.
Pea soup, made from a recipe handed down in Juliette's family, went on the menu three months later.
Their son Robert later called himself Pea Soup Andersen, and the mascots Hap-pea and Pea-wee, two cartoon chefs splitting peas with a hammer and chisel, came from a cartoon by Charles Forbell.
Opening day in Santa Nella drew more than 10,000 customers, and the 77-foot windmill still turns whenever the restaurant is open.

Its California Korean War Veterans Memorial, set up in 1998, is a circle of 16 granite pillars, each five feet tall, engraved with the names of the 2,495 Californians who died in the Korean War.
An 11th Airborne memorial, dedicated in 2002, honors all airborne forces, and a small museum on the grounds displays uniforms and medals.

Boxer Mac Foster, a Marine sergeant, is buried here too.

Later the ground beneath it sank, more than 6 feet along its southern 30 to 40 miles, and the changes in elevation were at first blamed on earthquakes.

Kesterson's 12 ponds were the temporary end of the San Luis Drain, planned to run 290 miles and carry away salty water from under west side fields.
Only 82 miles were built before work stopped in 1975, so the drainage collected at Kesterson and evaporated, concentrating selenium that had washed out of black shale in the Coast Ranges.
Birds hatched with missing or deformed eyes, beaks, wings and legs.
Cleanup crews filled 713 acres with about a million cubic yards of soil, and scientists now call selenium's path from rock to duck the Kesterson effect.

In March 1970 Gustine became the first place in California with a 9-1-1 emergency phone system.
The town is home to a festa steeped in Portuguese tradition that is described as the largest in the nation.
Gustine High School hosts what is called the longest-running basketball tournament in California.
The local Rotary Club puts it on, and it celebrated its 75th year in 2017.

In May 1868 the naturalist John Muir crossed the river here on his long walk from Oakland to Yosemite.
Simon Newman's company store stood in Hills Ferry, and the building later served as Fisher's Opera House until it was torn down in 1904.
In July 1906 a fire near Hills Ferry and Newman burned 2,500 acres of wheat and barley and 20,000 acres of pasture.
By 1976, not even the shadows of a ghost town were left.

Orestimba Creek, which comes down from the Diablo Range near here, has the largest watershed of the 13 streams that feed the San Joaquin from its west side.
Its name was first written down as Arroyo de Orestimac in 1810, in the diary of Padre Jose Viader, the longtime head of Mission Santa Clara.
The creek watered the Mexican-era Rancho Orestimba y Las Garzas, whose ranch house stood above a sycamore grove on its banks.
In 1998 The Nature Conservancy bought the 33,000-acre Simon Newman Ranch in the hills upstream, and it still manages the land.

Most almond varieties cannot pollinate themselves, so growers plant a mix of varieties and count on bees to carry pollen between them.
Pollination brokers hire migratory beekeepers from at least 49 states for the job.
In 2017 California had about a million acres of almonds, which produced 2.25 billion pounds of shelled nuts.
When colony collapse disorder caused a shortage of honey bees around the turn of this century, government scientists developed almond trees that can pollinate themselves.

Crows Landing itself began as a landing on the San Joaquin River, started by John Crow, who came west from Missouri by covered wagon.

In 1887 the town moved four miles west to be on the Southern Pacific railroad, and members of the Crow family still farm walnuts there.
During the war the Navy ran ten liberty buses a day to Modesto and Patterson for its sailors, who were allowed to use the swimming pool at Patterson High School.

John D. Patterson bought it in 1866 for 5,400 dollars, and by his death in 1902 his holdings had grown to 18,462 acres.

Many of the canyon's place names, like Hideout Canyon and Murderers Gulch, recall Gold Rush bandits, and Joaquin Murrieta is said to have hidden wild mustangs up Adobe Creek before driving them to Sonora.
In June 1862, William Brewer camped in the canyon and wrote in his book Up and Down California of meeting a herd of thirty or forty antelope, as fleet as the wind.
A spring up the canyon, Adobe Springs, gives magnesium-rich water that is sold to the 7 Up bottling plant in Modesto.
Del Puerto Canyon Road follows the creek west into the mountains.

The fires reached Lick Observatory on Mount Hamilton on August 20, but the telescope domes did not burn.
Two of its three zones, the Canyon and Calaveras zones, grew together into a single fire.
In all, 222 buildings were destroyed and six people were hurt, but no one died.
A year later, a study of 6,000 acres of East Bay parkland found that the burn had been mostly good for the land:
its moderate to low heat spared most trees, renewed the plants and set off the sprouting of rare fire poppies.

Waste tires had been stockpiled at the Westley site since the 1960s and were used to fuel a waste-to-energy operation.
The fire poured tons of smoke and pollutants into the air and threatened surface water and groundwater.

In April 2000 the state sued the landowners, waste tire haulers and waste-to-energy operators to make them pay for the cleanup, saying workers had failed to quickly turn on the site's water cannon and foam systems.
Attorney General Bill Lockyer said the tire inferno left behind contaminated soil and threats to groundwater.

The Chochenyo-speaking Ohlone call the mountain Tuyshtak, meaning at the dawn of time, and in Miwok and Ohlone tradition it was the place of creation.
Most of the mountain, including its peak, was the homeland of the Volvon, a Bay Miwok-speaking people.
The mountain is still growing, pushed up by a hidden thrust fault beneath it.
In 1928 Standard Oil put a 10-million-candlepower aviation beacon on top, the Eye of Diablo, which could be seen for a hundred miles.
Every year since 1964, Pearl Harbor survivors and their families have relit the beacon on Pearl Harbor Day.

One stretch of I-580 is named the William Elton Brownie Brown Freeway, for a Tracy man who helped decide the route of I-5 through the San Joaquin Valley.
The piece between the I-205 split and this junction was built in the late 1960s and early 1970s on new right-of-way through low hills near Patterson.
That piece is an official state scenic highway, and so is I-5 from Highway 152 near Santa Nella to this junction, the only stretch of I-5 the state has named a scenic highway.
The junction sits in San Joaquin County, just north of the Stanislaus County line.

During World War Two, Vernalis had a Navy airfield, Naval Auxiliary Air Station Vernalis, along with a reconditioning center and a camp for prisoners of war.
San Joaquin City, near where the Stanislaus River joins the San Joaquin, was probably the largest of the boomtowns that sprang up after the Gold Rush.
It was founded in 1851 and kept its size until 1880, when competition from Stockton drew its trade away.

A nonprofit, River Partners, led the planting of about 400,000 native trees across 1,700 acres of the river's floodplain, one of California's largest projects to bring back streamside forest.
Swainson's hawks nest in the tall cottonwoods, and herons and cormorants nest together in big oaks on Christman Island.
Endangered riparian brush rabbits, raised in captivity, have been returned to their old habitat here.
From autumn through spring, big flocks of geese and sandhill cranes gather on the refuge.

After the final battle, soldiers executed four captured men, and an investigation found one soldier guilty.
Mexico never again tried to control the eastern San Joaquin Valley, and the river was renamed in his honor.
Estanislao was pardoned in 1829, and he spent his last years at Mission San Jose teaching others the Yokuts language and culture until his death in 1838.

In 1869 Banta became a stop on the new Western Pacific Railroad, part of the transcontinental line's route from Sacramento over Altamont Pass to the Bay Area.
In 1878 the railroad built its new junction at Tracy instead, and Banta became a quiet village at the far edge of the rail yards.
The Banta Inn, established in 1879, is said by some locals to be haunted.
Steve Perry, later the lead singer of Journey, once called Banta home, and his band Alien Project formed there in the mid-1970s.

Three miles west was the railroad town of Ellis, a coaling station where helper engines were kept to push trains over Altamont Pass; by 1870 it had about 45 buildings.
Once the railroad moved its facilities to the new Tracy station, railroad families and businesses followed, and Ellis faded.
In 1894 the railroad's local headquarters moved from Lathrop to Tracy, and a roundhouse followed in 1896.
By the 1950s farming had become Tracy's main business, and since the 1970s Bay Area growth spilling over the Altamont has made the railroad town a city of more than 90,000.
This is Yokuts homeland, and Yokuts people still live in the region.

Farming became the county's main business in the 1870s, as the Gold Rush economy faded, helped by the reclaiming of Delta marshland that began in 1869.
In 2024 its farms produced about 3.1 billion dollars' worth of crops and livestock.
The county grows about half of California's cherries, and its more than a dozen cherry packing houses handle nearly all the cherries grown in the state.
It is also home to one of the largest walnut processing plants in the world, a major handler of Livermore red walnuts, a variety developed in the San Joaquin Valley.

Long before the railroad, a sharp bend slowed the river here and made a shallow ford, a favorite fishing ground of the Yokuts, whose homeland this is.
The Spanish called it El Pescadero, the fishing place.
In 1848 John Doak and Jacob Bonsell started the first ferry across the San Joaquin here, pulling a barge along a rope stretched from shore to shore.

William Moss, a former Ohio riverboat captain, bought the ferry in 1856, and the valley beside it became Moss' Dale.
By August 1869 about 600 men were building the railroad bridge, 500 of them Chinese.
A reporter wrote that the last rail went down at 3 in the afternoon, just before the first train crossed.
The wooden swing bridge was rebuilt in steel in 1895 and replaced with today's lift bridge in 1942.

Joshua Cowell, the town's founder, brought dairy farming to the area.
The railroad stop was first called Cowell Station, but the line had a second Cowell Station, named for his brother Henry, so a new name was needed.
A local legend says residents chose the name Monteca and the railroad misprinted it, but a local columnist points out that the word monteca is nowhere to be found in Spanish dictionaries.
When Manteca incorporated in 1918, Cowell was elected its first mayor.
As recently as the 1970s Manteca lived mostly on farming.
Rising Bay Area home prices then turned it into a commuter town, and its population has more than tripled since 1980.

By 1871 Lathrop was an important division point and rail stop, and the railroad built a $50,000 hotel here, said to be one of the largest in California at the time.
In the 1880s the railroad moved its roundhouse and machine shop to Tracy, and Lathrop began a decline that lasted nearly 50 years, with a major fire in 1911 along the way.

Built in 1923, Flying Scotsman was the first steam locomotive officially clocked at 100 miles per hour, and it retired from regular service in 1963 after running more than 2 million miles.

Businessman Alan Pegler bought it and, with support from the British government, sent it touring the United States and Canada from 1969 to promote British exports, fitted with a cowcatcher, a bell and an American-style whistle.
The tour ran 15,400 miles, but some states treated the steam engine as a fire hazard, and in 1972 Pegler, deep in debt, declared bankruptcy.
After the engine sat at Sharpe Depot, businessman William McAlpine paid the debts and bought it for $72,000.
It sailed home through the Panama Canal, landed at Liverpool in February 1973 and steamed to Derby along a route lined with crowds.

Its Spanish name, Campo de los Franceses, the field of the Frenchmen, lived on in a Mexican land grant of 1844.

That trail later became an alternate route for the Mariposa Road, favored in the rainy season because it drained so well, and it survives as French Camp Road.

One founder, Jawala Singh, was a successful potato farmer who worked a 500-acre ranch next to Stockton with his partner Wasakha Singh.

The gurdwara also paid for the university studies of Dalip Singh Saund, who later became the first Sikh American and the first Asian American elected to Congress.
