The freeway threads the East Los Angeles Interchange in Boyle Heights, runs through Lincoln Heights, the city's first suburb, and crosses the Los Angeles River where the Arroyo Seco joins it, beside the wooded hills of Elysian Park.
The freeway follows the Los Angeles River through the Glendale Narrows, with the brushy hills of Griffith Park on the west side.
Studios, the airport and the neighborhoods of Glendale, Burbank and Sun Valley spread across the flat east end of the San Fernando Valley, below the rocky Verdugo Mountains.
Tujunga Wash, a mostly dry riverbed in this part of the valley, usually carries much water only during storms between November and April.
Pacoima, Mission Hills and Sylmar fill the north end of the valley, once a land of mission vineyards, wheat and olive groves, with the San Gabriel Mountains rising close by.
Snow almost never falls on the valley floor, but the mountains of the Angeles National Forest above Sylmar are capped with snow every winter.
Newhall Pass, between the San Gabriel and Santa Susana Mountains, links the San Fernando Valley with the Santa Clarita Valley, where Newhall grew up as a railroad and oil town.
Summer heat in the pass can top 100 degrees.
Snow is possible here from December to February, but it is quite uncommon.
Planned neighborhoods of Valencia spread along the Santa Clara River, with Magic Mountain's roller coasters on the hills west of the freeway.
In April and May, chaparral yucca send up flower stalks 3 to 10 feet tall.
Castaic and the Five Mile Grade.
North of Castaic, the long Five Mile Grade leads into the Angeles National Forest, where the freeway crosses the Sierra Pelona Mountains between Castaic Lake and Pyramid Lake.
Ice and snow sometimes lead the Highway Patrol to close the 40 miles of I-5 between Castaic and Grapevine.
Pyramid Lake fills the canyon of Piru Creek west of the freeway in the Sierra Pelona Mountains, and farther north the land opens into Peace Valley around Gorman.
From mid-April through May, Hungry Valley near Gorman offers guided wildflower tours.
Tejon Pass sits among the open hills of Tejon Ranch around Lebec.
When snow and ice close the freeway over the pass, the shutdown usually lasts four to six hours, but some closures run longer than a day.
Spring brings showy wildflower blooms to Tejon Ranch, where several of California's natural regions meet.
Grapevine Canyon carries the freeway's long, steep grade past Fort Tejon's centuries-old valley oaks to the southern edge of the San Joaquin Valley.
Autumn was acorn harvest time for the Kitanemuk people, whose homeland includes these mountains.
Wheeler Ridge and the valley's edge.
Below the Grapevine the land flattens at Wheeler Ridge, where the Tehachapi and San Emigdio mountains meet the floor of the San Joaquin Valley and Highway 99 meets I-5.
In spring, Wind Wolves Preserve in the hills to the southwest holds a nature festival with guided hikes and wildflower viewing.
Flat farmland covers the old beds of Kern Lake and Buena Vista Lake, with the San Emigdio Mountains forming the valley's southern wall and the oil country of Maricopa and Taft off to the west.
Kern County's valley floor here is farm country, where almonds and pistachios are among the most valuable crops, and Highways 119 and 43 lead west to the oil towns of Taft and Maricopa.
Kern River and the Elk Hills.
The freeway crosses the Kern River near the Kern Water Bank's recharge basins and runs past the low, bare Elk Hills.
Late summer is when the tule elk at the state reserve off Stockdale Highway become most active.
The elk stay most active into early autumn.
Around Buttonwillow, known locally as cotton country, farm fields and big power lines spread across the valley floor, with the Temblor Range on the far western skyline.
Oil pumps dot the low Lost Hills west of the freeway, the aqueduct runs past the town of Lost Hills, and Kern National Wildlife Refuge lies out on the flats to the east.
North of the Kern County line, the old bed of Tulare Lake, now farmland, spreads east of the freeway.
In very wet winters, like 2023, storms can bring Tulare Lake back, flooding the old lakebed east of the freeway.
The Kettleman Hills, with their oil field, rise west of the freeway.
The freeway runs through the West Side farmland of Fresno County, which in 2022 led California counties in the value of its almonds, pistachios, garlic and processing tomatoes.
Wide-open farmland stretches east of the freeway, with the oil field ridges around Coalinga and the Diablo Range to the west, and the big Harris Ranch feedlot beside the freeway.
Summers around Coalinga are very hot and dry, and most of its 8 inches of yearly rain falls from October to May.
Big farms of Westlands Water District spread across the valley floor here, growing crops such as almonds, tomatoes, pistachios and wheat, with the three Joaquin Rocks on the ridge to the west.
The low Panoche Hills rise close on the west with the higher Diablo Range beyond them.
The grasslands of Panoche Valley, beyond the hills, are critical habitat, especially in winter, for golden eagles, hawks and mountain plovers.
The aqueduct runs through flat farmland, with the San Joaquin River and the town of Firebaugh well off to the east and the Panoche Hills to the west.
Firebaugh's yearly Cantaloupe Round-Up celebrates the melon harvest, which peaks in late July.
Pumping plants, power lines and canals line the west side of the valley here, while the Grasslands spread along the San Joaquin River north and east of Los Banos.
Each autumn more than 20,000 cranes and 60,000 geese arrive at Merced National Wildlife Refuge to stay about six months.
Wildflowers bloom in rings around the drying vernal pools of Merced National Wildlife Refuge.
The state and federal water projects meet here and share San Luis Reservoir, its dam and its forebay.
In the wet season, from about November to April, water to spare is pumped from O'Neill Forebay up into San Luis Reservoir.
Farms spread east across Merced and Stanislaus counties toward the old railroad towns of Gustine and Newman and the San Joaquin River.
Newman holds its yearly Fall Festival on Labor Day weekend.

The Diablo Range rises close on the west, cut by Del Puerto Canyon, while Patterson, known for its distribution centers, sits east of the freeway, and on clear days Mount Diablo shows on the northwest skyline.
Downtown Patterson hosts its Apricot Fiesta on the first weekend of June.
North of the I-580 junction, the freeway crosses flat San Joaquin County farmland near the edge of the Delta, between the San Joaquin River and the old railroad towns of Banta and Tracy.
From autumn through spring, flocks of geese and sandhill cranes gather at the San Joaquin River refuge east of the freeway.
The freeway crosses the San Joaquin River at Mossdale and runs through Lathrop, a railroad town where large planned neighborhoods now spread west of the freeway.
I-5 runs through Stockton, past the deepwater port and its channel to San Francisco Bay, and crosses the Calaveras River.
Nearly all of Stockton's rain falls from October through April.
Summers here are very hot and dry.
Lodi vineyards and the Delta's edge.
Vineyards spread east toward Lodi, while the flat, reclaimed islands of the Delta, held in by levees, stretch off to the west.
Cranes, geese and swans use the Woodbridge reserve as their winter home.
Wetlands of the Cosumnes River Preserve lie near the freeway, which runs along the eastern edge of the Stone Lakes refuge as it passes through Elk Grove.
Along the river to Land Park.
The freeway runs close to the Sacramento River through the south side of Sacramento, near William Land Park and the zoo.
I-5 runs between downtown and the river, past Old Sacramento and the Tower Bridge.
The airport and the Sacramento River.
North of downtown the freeway passes the old ARCO Arena site and the airport and crosses the Sacramento River.
Between floods, much of the Yolo Bypass is farmed, mostly in rice.
In wet winters and springs, the bypass floods and becomes a huge wetland for birds and young salmon.
The freeway passes Woodland, a farm town with a big tomato cannery, and crosses Cache Creek beside the little town of Yolo.
Farm country continues past Zamora and Dunnigan, near the Dunnigan Hills, and on clear days the Sutter Buttes rise from the valley floor to the north.
Almonds, rice and the Sutter Buttes.
Almond orchards ring Arbuckle and rice fields spread across the flat valley floor, while the Sutter Buttes rise from the plain to the east.
Ducks and geese arrive in fall, and many rice fields are flooded to give them food and shelter through the winter.
Rice fields spread across the valley here, and the marshes of the Sacramento National Wildlife Refuge sit just east of the freeway.
Waterfowl numbers at the refuge peak in late November and early December.
In April, shorebirds and songbirds stop at the refuge on their way north.
Most of the refuge marshes are dry in summer, with only about 15 percent of the wetlands flooded.
North of Willows, almond orchards grow around Artois.
Orchards of almonds, walnuts, prunes and olives grow around Orland and Corning, and the freeway crosses Stony Creek and Thomes Creek.
Thomes Creek runs highest in February, on average.
The wide gravel bed of Thomes Creek is often dry in summer.
The Corning Olive Festival is held on the second Saturday in October.
This is the northern end of a band of farmland that runs almost unbroken to Bakersfield, and on clear days Lassen Peak stands on the eastern skyline.
The Red Bluff Round-Up rodeo comes to town in late April.
Red Bluff averages about 100 days a year with highs of 90 degrees or more.
Between Red Bluff and Cottonwood, mildly rugged rangeland separates the valley's crop areas.
Near the northern tip of the Central Valley, the freeway passes Cottonwood and Anderson, with ranch land along Cottonwood Creek.
Cottonwood Creek often runs like a large river in winter and spring.
By summer and fall, Cottonwood Creek dwindles to a trickle.
Redding sits at the northwestern end of the Central Valley, with mountains on the north, east and west and farmland to the south.
The average July high in Redding is near 100 degrees.
Winter brings most of Redding's rain, often with fog, and at times snow.
North Redding and the dam towns.
Here Redding's northern edge meets the city of Shasta Lake, with Shasta Dam a few miles west.
Summers here are hot and dry, with big swings between daytime highs and nighttime lows.
The freeway crosses Shasta Lake, whose steep shores are covered with tall evergreens and manzanita.
Summer is the busy season at Bridge Bay, the lake's largest marina.
The freeway follows a steep, forested canyon, past old stage stops and Gold Rush camps.
North of Redding, snow can fall at higher elevations from fall to spring, and Caltrans sometimes requires chains.
Granite spires rise west of the freeway, and an old railroad town fills the canyon bottom.
Dunsmuir gets about 63 inches of rain and snow a year, about three and a half times as much as Yreka or Medford.
More than half of Dunsmuir's yearly rain and snow falls in December, January and February.
Dunsmuir's last freeze comes around April 24 in an average year.
In summer, Dunsmuir stocks the river in town with trophy rainbow trout up to 14 pounds.
The first freeze usually arrives around October 20.
The canyon opens onto the foot of the volcano, with the city of Mount Shasta, the dark cone of Black Butte and Black Butte Summit.
In February 1959 the old Ski Bowl on Mount Shasta got 15.75 feet of snow in one storm, a U.S. record.
Climbers head for Mount Shasta's summit from late April into October.
Weed grew up around lumber mills.
Hot flows from Shastina's eruptions once covered the ground here, and recent wildfires have left their marks.
Weed holds its Carnevale, with bocce ball tournaments, each June or July.
A wide, dry valley in the rain shadow of the Klamath Mountains, dotted with hummocks, with hay fields, cattle and juniper.
Summer rain almost never falls here, except for an occasional thunderstorm.
Winters are cool to cold, with fairly frequent snow.
Gold Rush country around the county seat, with the Klamath Mountains rising to the west and the Shasta River cutting north toward the Klamath.
Yreka holds Gold Rush Days every June.
Yreka averages only about 12 inches of snow a year, mostly from November through February.
Klamath River to the Oregon line.
Below the old Iron Gate Dam site, the Klamath runs through an arid valley of farms and ranches.
To the north rise the Siskiyou Mountains, the divide between the Klamath and the Rogue.
Just over the Oregon line, Siskiyou Summit usually gets snow from November through April.

Active Catholic parish of the Archdiocese of Los Angeles, run by the Claretian Missionaries, with a museum.

Which mission was the first one founded in Alta California, in 1769?
Mission San Diego de Alcalá was founded on July 16, 1769.
It began on a hill by the harbor and moved to its present site in 1774.
Toypurina, a Tongva medicine woman, helped organize what at Mission San Gabriel in 1785?
The first school in Los Angeles.
A trade fair with other missions.
The planting of the first vineyard.
Toypurina helped organize the 1785 revolt after baptized Tongva people were banned from holding their dances.
It failed, and she was sent to a distant mission.
What brought down the Great Stone Church at Mission San Juan Capistrano in 1812?
An earthquake on December 8, 1812 collapsed the church during Mass, and about 40 people died.
What destroyed the church at Mission San Fernando in 1971?
The 1971 San Fernando earthquake destroyed the church.
It was rebuilt by 1974, while the long convento from 1822 survived.
Pablo Tac, born at Mission San Luis Rey, created the first written form of which language?
He studied in Rome and made a way to write the Luiseño language.
His work was the only primary source in Luiseño written by a Luiseño until the twentieth century.
About how many vehicles enter the United States at the San Ysidro border crossing on a typical day?
About 70,000 vehicles and 20,000 people on foot come north through San Ysidro each day.
In 1915, San Diego offered Charles Hatfield $10,000 to do what?
The self-styled rainmaker was to fill a reservoir, and the 1916 storms that followed broke the Lower Otay Dam.
What did artists paint on the freeway and bridge pillars of Chicano Park?
Chicano Park has the largest collection of outdoor murals in the United States, painted on the concrete pillars.
Which famous airplane was built in San Diego in 1927?
The Spirit of St. Louis was built in San Diego for Charles Lindbergh's 1927 flight across the Atlantic, and the city named its airport Lindbergh Field.
Besides Torrey Pines, the only other wild Torrey pines grow on which island?
A related kind of Torrey pine grows wild in two groves on Santa Rosa Island, off Santa Barbara.
The town of Del Mar was named after what?
Ella Loop named it after Bayard Taylor's poem The Fight of Paso del Mar.
Which famous singer stood at the main gate to greet fans when the Del Mar racetrack opened in 1937?
Bing Crosby helped found the track and welcomed about 15,000 fans on opening day.
What kind of flower blooms across the Carlsbad Flower Fields each spring?
The fields are 55 acres of Giant Tecolote ranunculus, blooming from early March into early May.
In the 1970s, what surprising birds showed up at Buena Vista Lagoon?
Locals thought the flamingos had escaped from the San Diego Zoo, but the zoo said none were missing.
Which TV hero had episodes filmed at Mission San Luis Rey in 1957?
Disney's Zorro series filmed scenes there, with the mission standing in for Mission San Gabriel.
Las Pulgas Road on Camp Pendleton is named after what?
Las pulgas is Spanish for the fleas, which bit a mission survey party that camped in the canyon.
The rare Pacific pocket mouse, which lives on Camp Pendleton, is more closely related to which animal than to mice?
Despite its name, it belongs to the family Heteromyidae, which makes it a closer relative of beavers than of true mice.
San Onofre is Spanish for Saint Onuphrius.
The area was named for Saint Onuphrius, a hermit from fourth-century Egypt.
What is the famous surf spot Trestles named after?
Surfers named it for the wooden railroad trestle over San Mateo Creek that they walked under to reach the beach.
Where do the swallows of Capistrano spend the winter?
The cliff swallows winter around Goya, Argentina, and fly about 6,000 miles north each spring.
Trabuco Creek is named for something a Portolá expedition soldier lost in 1769.
Trabuco is Spanish for blunderbuss, a kind of old shotgun, and the gun was never found.
El Toro, the old name of Lake Forest, means what in Spanish?
El Toro means the bull; the town became the city of Lake Forest in 1991.
Jamboree Road is named for what 1953 event?
The 1953 National Scout Jamboree was held on Irvine Ranch land, and the road that served it was renamed Jamboree Road.
What were Tustin's giant wooden hangars built to hold during World War II?
The Navy built them for blimps that patrolled the coast in World War II.
About how many panes of glass cover the Crystal Cathedral, now Christ Cathedral?
The building has 10,000 rectangular panes, mirrored outside and see-through inside.
The name Anaheim joins Ana, for the Santa Ana River, with a German word meaning what?
The German founders named it Annaheim, home by the Santa Ana River.
When Cordelia Knott began serving fried chicken in June 1934, how many dinners did she serve?
She served eight fried chicken dinners at 65 cents each; today the restaurant serves more than 1.5 million a year.
Who is the mascot on the 1959 sign at the oldest McDonald's, in Downey?
Speedee, a little hamburger-headed chef, was McDonald's mascot before Ronald McDonald.
How did workers fill orders in the giant Sears mail-order building in Boyle Heights?
Workers roller-skated around the building and sent items down corkscrew slides to trucks and trains.
In 1896, Griffith J. Griffith gave Los Angeles the first 3,015 acres of Griffith Park as what kind of present?
He gave the land on December 16, 1896, as a Christmas gift to the people of Los Angeles.
During World War II, how was Lockheed's aircraft factory in Burbank hidden from the air?
It was moved into a cave.
It was painted to look like a lake.
It was covered by a painted tarp showing a neighborhood.
It was hidden inside a movie studio.
A huge painted tarp, rubber cars and fake trees of chicken wire and feathers made it look like a quiet neighborhood.
Which rock and roll pioneer grew up in Pacoima?
Ritchie Valens was born in Pacoima in 1941 and turned La Bamba into a hit in 1958.
Sylmar's name blends Latin words for which two things?
Sylmar joins Latin words for forest and sea, for the sea of olive trees that once covered it.
What did William Mulholland say when Los Angeles Aqueduct water first arrived in 1913?
He spoke those words at the opening ceremony on November 5, 1913.
In 1842, Francisco López found gold in Placerita Canyon clinging to the roots of what?
He was gathering wild onions near an oak and found gold on their roots, six years before Sutter's Mill.
How long did the Pico Number 4 oil well keep producing before it was capped?
It struck oil in 1876 and was capped in 1990, 114 years later.

From a pyramid-shaped rock left by road builders.
From an ancient pyramid under the water.

The name came from a dead badger found in 1806 at the mouth of a canyon about 15 miles northeast of today's pass.
Starting in 1858, which unusual animals did the Army test at Fort Tejon?
Fort Tejon was the western end of the Army's experimental Camel Corps.
How high does the Edmonston Pumping Plant lift water to get it over the Tehachapi Mountains?
Edmonston lifts the water 1,926 feet, the most powerful water lift in the world apart from pumped-storage power plants.
How long did the 1910 Lakeview Gusher keep spilling oil?
It gushed for about 18 months and released roughly 9 million barrels of oil.
Before it was named for President Taft, what did the railroad call the station at Taft?
The railroad named it Moron because Moro might be confused with Morro Bay; it was renamed Taft in 1909.
In the 1870s, when tule elk were thought to be extinct, where were the last few found?
On an island in San Francisco Bay.
Hiding in the tules near Buena Vista Lake.
On top of the Tehachapi Mountains.
In 1874 a game warden, tipped off by Henry Miller, found the survivors hiding in the tules near Buena Vista Lake.
The tree that gave Buttonwillow its name is actually what kind of plant?
Despite the name, the landmark tree is a buttonbush, not a willow.
What has stayed within about 10 miles of Buttonwillow since 1970?
The hottest spot in the state.

The Temblor Range on the western skyline is named for a Spanish word.
Temblor is Spanish for tremor, fitting for mountains beside the San Andreas Fault.
What were the drillers looking for when they found the Lost Hills oil field in 1910?
They were drilling a water well for livestock and struck oil at 530 feet.
Kettleman City is close to the halfway point between Los Angeles and which city?
Exit 309 sits near the halfway point between Los Angeles and San Francisco or Sacramento.

A salty bay of the Pacific Ocean.
A crater lake in an old volcano.

The name Avenal comes from Spanish.
Spanish soldiers and explorers named it for the wild oats that covered the plain.
Coalinga got its name from what?

Her Iron Zoo turned nodding oil pump jacks into animals and characters, like a zebra and a bobbing goat, to draw drivers off I-5.

The walls of an old fort.

most of its water is pumped in from canals instead of flowing in from a river.
The biggest striped bass ever caught in California came out of O'Neill Forebay in 2008.
About how much did it weigh?
The fish, caught on August 5, 2008, was 52 and a half inches long and weighed 70.6 pounds.
Santa Nella's name comes from a Spanish word meaning what?
It is an English mangling of centinela, sentinel, from the old Rancho de Centinela.
The first Andersen's cafe, opened in 1924, was named in honor of what?
It was called Andersen's Electrical Cafe, after the couple's proudest possession, a new electric stove.
What poisoned the water birds at Kesterson Reservoir in the 1980s?
Selenium from Coast Range shale built up in farm drainage water that evaporated in the ponds.
In 1970, Gustine became the first place in California to have what?
California's first 9-1-1 system was installed in Gustine in March 1970.
About how many beehives are trucked into California's almond orchards each February?
Over a million hives, nearly half of all the hives in the country, come for the bloom.
Thomas Patterson laid out his town's circles and spoke-like streets after which two cities?
He wanted Patterson to look different from other farm towns, so he modeled it on Washington, D.C., and Paris.
The name Vernalis comes from a Latin word meaning what?
Vernalis is Latin for springlike, and a local historian said it was named for two ranchers' daughters, Verna and Alice.
Manteca, the name of a dairy town, is Spanish for what?
Manteca means lard, an odd name for a town whose railroad stop shipped dairy products.
Which famous British steam locomotive was hidden from creditors at an Army depot in Lathrop in 1972?
Its bankrupt owner stored Flying Scotsman at Sharpe Depot until a new owner paid the debts and shipped it home.
French Camp's other old name, Castoria, comes from the Latin word for which animal?
Castor is Latin for beaver, a nod to the camp's role in the fur trade.
The Calaveras River has a Spanish name.
Calaveras means skulls; the river is said to be named for skulls a Spanish expedition found on its banks in 1806.
Benjamin Holt's 1904 track-type tractor gave its name to which company?
A company photographer reportedly said the machine crawled like a caterpillar, and Holt adopted the name.
In what year did the final stretch of I-5 open, just north of Stockton?
The last 4.6 miles opened on October 12, 1979, completing the freeway from Mexico to Canada.
Which drink was first sold in Lodi in 1919?
Roy Allen sold his first batch of A&W Root Beer from a cart during a parade in Lodi.
About how many miles of levees ring the Delta's islands?
About 1,100 miles of levees protect the Delta's islands, many of which sit below sea level.
In Plains Miwok, Mokelumne means people of the what?
Moke means fishnet and umne means people of.
How was the Tower Bridge's gold color chosen?
By a vote of local residents.

What giant animal sculpture is inside Terminal B at Sacramento's airport?
Leap, a 56-foot red rabbit by the artist Lawrence Argent, is in Terminal B.

The Sutter Buttes are the leftovers of what?

Glenn owned about 55,000 acres and was nicknamed California's Wheat King.
What was the town of Artois called before 1918?
Germantown was renamed Artois in 1918, during World War One, after a region of France.
Orland calls itself the North American capital of what?
In 2017 Orland declared itself the Queen Bee Capital of North America because of its many queen bee producers.
Besides Mount St. Helens, which volcano in the lower 48 states erupted in the 20th century?
Lassen Peak's eruptions began in 1914, and its biggest blast came on May 22, 1915.
How long did William Ide's California Republic last?
The California Republic lasted from June 14 to July 9, 1846.
What was the river town of Bend first called?
It started as Horsethief Bend, became Sander's Bend, and was finally shortened to Bend.
What makes Cottonwood Creek special among the Sacramento River's tributaries?
It is the largest undammed one.
As the largest undammed tributary of the Sacramento, it is known for its Chinook salmon and steelhead runs.
What was Redding called during the Gold Rush?
The ground held so little gold that the spot was called Poverty Flats.
Why doesn't the Sundial Bridge touch the Sacramento River?

How long was the conveyor belt that carried rock to build Shasta Dam?

What is the Pit River named for?
Pits its people dug for homes and to trap game.
The name comes from the pits the Pit River people dug for winter homes and as traps for game that came to drink at the river.
About how high above the old Pit River was the Pit River Bridge built?
It stands about 500 feet above the old riverbed, though a full lake comes within about 40 feet of the bridge.
Which baseball legend played an exhibition game in Dunsmuir in 1924?
Babe Ruth and Bob Meusel played the locals in the city park on a barnstorming tour.
Which soft drink brand got its start at natural springs just north of Dunsmuir?
Springs at the old Shasta Springs resort were the original source of the Shasta brand of soft drinks.
How much snow fell at the old Mount Shasta Ski Bowl in a single February 1959 storm?
The 15.75 feet that fell from February 13 to 19, 1959, set the U.S. record for snow in one storm.
Mount Shasta rises 14,179 feet, the second-highest peak in the Cascades.
Why did Abner Weed pick this spot for his lumber mill?
He found that the area's strong winds helped dry lumber.
In 1941, State of Jefferson rebels promised to secede how often?
Their proclamation said they would secede every Thursday until further notice.
According to Mark Twain, where did the name Yreka come from?
Twain said a bakery sign seen from behind read YREKA, but the name really comes from the Shasta word for Mount Shasta.
How many hydroelectric dams were torn down on the Klamath River in 2023 and 2024?
Four dams came out, the largest dam removal in U.S. history.
